item.title: Venice Biennale Awards Selected by Public Vote Go to Nick Cave, Indian Pavilion - ARTnews.com
item.description:
After a Venice Biennale of bitter controversy, the exhibition has at last revealed the winners of its top honors, which were chosen this year by public vote instead of a jury of esteemed curators because that panel resigned in protest. This time around, the awards went to the American artist Nick Cave for his participation in Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition and India for its national pavilion.

Dubbed the Visitors’ Lions, these awards replaced the Golden Lions, which are regularly given to participants in the main exhibition and artists representing countries with pavilions in the exhibition. This time around, just two awards were given out, one for an artist in the main show and one for a national pavilion.

The Biennale was forced to instate the Visitors’ Lions after the five-person Golden Lion jury resigned in May, in advance of the show’s opening. By that point, the curators had already said that they would “refrain from considering those countries whose leaders are currently charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court,” a move that would exclude Israel and Russia from consideration. More than half of the artists in the main show said they would not accept the Visitors’ Lions in solidarity.

Cave’s contributions to the Kouoh’s show, titled “In Minor Keys,” included a decidedly major work: Amalgam (Origin), a 26-foot-tall bronze sculpture in which a person’s body sprouts branches and wildlife. The work, which appeared outdoors at the Arsenale, derived from a similar-looking proposal for a piece to replace a toppled Confederate monument.

Inside and outside the Arsenale, there were yet more large-scale Cave sculptures that composed Two Points in Time – At Once, which featured more figures whose bodies fuse with plants. Needlepointed portraits accompanied those figures. “The works address the stages of grief toward mourning, rebirth, and radical connection,” Cave wrote on social media in May, when the Biennale opened.

India’s pavilion, titled “Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home,” dealt largely with how objects act as vessels for memories and featured such grandly sized pieces as Sumakshi Singh’s Permanent Address, in which the walls of a house were remade in see-through thread, causing the domicile to appear flimsy and impermanent.

Alongside Singh, the pavilion featured works by Alwar Balasubramaniam, Ranjani Shettar, Asim Waqif, and Skarma Sonam Tashi. Organized by curator Amin Jaffer, the pavilion was the first staged by India at the Biennale since 2019.

The Biennale’s spare release unusually did not include citations for why the Indian Pavilion and Cave won, likely because neither had been selected by a jury. Instead, the release included a statement from Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, who said, “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition – the Visitors’ Award – as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it. I can say without hesitation that La Biennale is brimming with ever-renewed energy thanks to the vibrant presence of everyone.”

When the Biennale opened, dozens of participants in Kouoh’s main exhibition, as well as several dozen more with national pavilions, signed a statement saying that they did not want to be considered for the Visitors’ Lions as a form of solidarity with the resigned jury. If these artists were selected as winners, they said, the Biennale could expect legal action. “Not only is this confusing for visitors, it is blatantly disrespectful towards the artists who have made the request for removal of their names,” the artists said in a statement.

Though it did not directly respond to the artists, the Biennale said in its release about the Visitors’ Lions that “all national participations” were eligible, since the exhibition is about “openness, dialogue, and the rejection of any form of closure or censorship.”

Notably, neither Cave nor the artists representing India signed the e-flux statement, which was endorsed by many of the artists with most talked-about pavilions in Venice—including Florentina Holzinger, whose Austrian Pavilion generated long lines and emerged as an early favorite during the professional preview.

The Visitors’ Lions bring to an end a tumultuous Biennale marked by protests over Israel and Russia’s pavilions, which faced an outcry both before and during the Biennale, with many calling for both countries to be ejected altogether. The Biennale sought to proclaim itself a neutral entity, saying that it cannot kick out any nation recognized as a state by the Italian government. But the logic proved unpersuasive for many, including the European Union, which said it will revoke a 2 million euro grant that it typically awards to the Biennale as a protest against the Russian Pavilion’s return this year, during a period when Russia continues to face EU sanctions over its war in Ukraine.

Lifetime achievement prizes are typically revealed ahead of the Biennale’s opening, but none were awarded this time because Kouoh, the curator of the main show, died in 2025 before she could select the winners. A Silver Lion, for a promising young artist in the main exhibition, was not awarded during this round, either, likely because that prize is given out by a jury who was not present to offer it.

The Biennale has positioned this year’s fraught edition as a resounding success. Upon its closure this past weekend, the Biennale said the show received more than 714,000 visitors, the second-highest attendance figure in the exhibition’s history. “This edition of the Biennale, so rich in events and complex developments—so immersed in the harsh affairs of the world—was pervaded by a vivid spirit, rewarded indeed by the number of visitors,” Buttafuoco, the Biennale president, said in a statement this past weekend.

The Biennale was initially expected to announce the Visitors’ Lions when the exhibition concluded its run on Sunday. Asked by ARTnews about the delay, a Biennale spokesperson said that extra time was necessary to “ensure that sufficient time is available to complete the necessary overall vote count.”

item.title: Thelma Golden Stepping Down as Studio Museum Director After 21 Years - Hyperallergic
item.description:
One year after the Studio Museum in Harlem's long-awaited reopening, Thelma Golden, 61, intends to step down after 21 years as the institution's director and chief curator. Golden will depart both roles once the museum appoints a replacement.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition — and as I look ahead to new projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a press statement regarding her decision.

Since assuming both titles in 2005, Golden has stimulated international and institutional recognition of Black, African, and diasporic African artists who are systematically overlooked in the Western canons of art history and modern and contemporary art. Prior to joining the Studio Museum, then led by Lowery Stokes Sims, Golden held curatorial roles at the Whitney Museum of American Art.

item.title: When a Ceramics Studio Becomes a Stage - Hyperallergic
item.description:
At the center of Matthew Lutz-Kinoy’s The Mud Room, a raised platform containing a large kiln, two ceramicists’ alcoves, and buckets of clay acts as a stage. The first play explored the intersections of farming, the kiln, and the emergence of the artspeak-adjacent locavore chef.

While Amant’s on-site restaurant served its own fare of purple radicchio and Block Island anchovies to the audience, seated in a perimeter around the action, the protagonist, Marin — a failed curator turned restaurateur in rural France — droned on about her hopes for a publisher to appreciate her culinary foray as a radical “linguistic concept” and “rhizomatic” project.

Meanwhile, four paintings surrounding the stage ridicule the posturing of the art-world types in the first performance. Directly opposite the entrance, monstrous figures swallow one another’s entrails and phallic appendages while exchanging the fruits of their labor: ceramics. To the right, Lutz-Kinoy’s “The Rose Garden” (2026) combines an homage to Keith Haring’s “Crack Is Wack” (1986) with silhouettes reminiscent of Aaron Douglas’s New Deal-era public commissions. Opposite it, another painting pays tribute to Douglas, as well as to Philip Guston and Reuben Kadish’s restored “The Struggle Against War and Fascism” (1934–35).

item.title: Military History Museum in Dresden Agrees to Return Contested Nazi-Era Family Archive to Jehovah’s Witnesses - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the New York Times. Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau.

At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website notes, given that her brothers lost their lives due to their pacifism.

The parties came to an “amicable agreement” on November 19, which was formalized the following day by the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The museum and the Jehovah’s Witnesses agreed to keep the details of the settlement private. A Kusserow relative told the New York Times it is “a great relief that at last we will have these precious documents back where Annemarie always wanted them.”

item.title: Bukhara Biennial Unveils ‘The Long Welcome’ Theme and Names First Artists - ARTnews.com
item.description:
After an inaugural edition last year, the Bukhara Biennial will return to Uzbekistan in 2027, this time with “The Long Welcome” as a theme (after 2025’s theme of “Recipes for Broken Hearts”). As announced this past summer, the artistic director for the next edition—slated to open September 3 and run through November 21—is Kulapat Yantrasast, the revered architect behind museum projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Louvre, Harvard Art Museums, and the Art Institute of Chicago (as well as others while he worked for Tadao Ando).

“At a time when the world needs dialogue and understanding more than ever, culture can bring people together and open space for a shared future,” Bukhara Biennial commissioner Gayane Umerova said in a press release announcing the theme, which will be organized around four parts: Local Hospitality, Co-Creation, Resilience and Biodiversity, and Living Heritage. “For centuries, Bukhara welcomed travelers, craftspeople and merchants from across the world, and that openness shaped its identity. Through the biennial, we want to carry this legacy forward through contemporary art, so that it becomes part of life in the city, creates opportunities for its residents and leaves a lasting cultural legacy.”

Yantrasast added: “The Long Welcome celebrates the spirit of hospitality that made Bukhara worth crossing continents to reach, and worth returning to again and again. When people welcome you into their city, you want to give something back. My hope is that an artist who returns to Bukhara years from now will find that something they made with people here has become part of everyday life.”

Along with news of the theme, the Bukhara Biennial announced its first slate of artists to exhibit work in the city, which will also host the 19th Annual Conference of UNESCO Creative Cities next year. Below, see the artists enlisted.

Anish Kapoor (India / UK)
Koo Jeong A (South Korea)
Sevara Haydarova Donazzan (Uzbekistan)
Susan Philipsz (UK / Germany)
Nigina Mirzadzhanova (Uzbekistan)
Precious Okoyomon (Nigeria / USA)
Ugo Rondinone (Switzerland)
Vivian Suter (Argentina / Switzerland / Guatemala)
Joseph Arzoumanov (France / Armenia)
Oscar Tuazon (USA)
Maksim Vardanyan and Daima Rakhmanbekova (Uzbekistan)
Huma Bhabha (Pakistan / USA)
Bethan Laura Wood (UK)

item.title: South African Curator and Artist Tamlin Blake Murdered at 51 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Visionary curator and mixed-media artist Tamlin Blake was found murdered in her Riebeek West home in South Africa on Sunday, November 22, at age 51.

West Coast District police confirmed that several of Blake's items were allegedly stolen and traced to a nearby farm. The 32-year-old suspect, who police have since arrested, had been released from prison less than a week before the incident, according to local outlets.

As the chief curator at Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based nonprofit dedicated to connecting South African artists with larger audiences and collectors, Blake conceived programs to help artists advance their careers. An artist herself, she explored themes of belonging, identity, and status in multiple exhibitions at Everard Read gallery, and fostered collaborations with the Spier Artisan Studio and the Keiskamma Art Project.

item.title: How Alison Luchs, the “Museum Rizzler,” Became Gen Z’s Goated Art Historian - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Lock in, chat, because we're about to drop some major lore on a new internet personality who puts every influencer to shame. During a recent kiki with Hyperallergic, designated baddie Alison Luchs, a curator of Early European sculpture and Deputy Head of Sculpture and Decorative Arts at the National Gallery of Art (NGA) in Washington, DC, gave us the deets on how she became a social media superstar overnight by using Gen Z lingo in an educational video series about collection objects.

This has been a goated year for Luchs, who has worked with the NGA for over four decades. Now known as the “Museum Rizzler,” the 78-year-old curator has garnered millions of views on her videos translating art and anthropological history into accessible stories for younger generations. Connecting centuries-old artifacts and mythologies to contemporary pop culture with terms like “chopped,” “sigma,” “aura points,” “gagged,” “popping off,” “chud,” and so on, Luchs has drawn a reverent audience that gassed her up so much she was honored with two Webby Awards.

Luchs and NGA's head of marketing and communications, Sydni Myers, broke down the making of the Museum Rizzler, the virtual and in-person impacts of the series' instant virality, and the behind-the-scenes process that goes into each video. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

item.title: Kate Jenkins Whips Up Delicious ‘Knitalian’ Dishes in an Immersive Exhibition - Colossal
item.description:
From plates of ravioli and spaghetti to bottles of chianti and sardines springing from their tins, Kate Jenkins‘ immersive art-meets-restaurant experience is something to really sink your teeth into. Known for her realistic knitted foodstuffs, the Brighton-based artist and knitwear designer presents Kate’s Knitalian at Air Contemporary, inviting us to consider the (rather unexpected) mouthwatering possibilities of yarn.

For the opening reception, visitors were required to reserve a spot much as one would do to book a table in a traditional restaurant, including two timed sittings. Everything from wheels of salami and tortellini to tiramisù and bottles of “Pinot Stitchio” fill the delicatessen experience in a celebration of Italian cuisine.

Kate’s Knitalian continues through December 22 in London. And if you find yourself in Brighton, you can visit the artist’s studio, which is open daily in Arundel Place. See more on Jenkins’ Instagram. You might also enjoy Lucy Sparrow’s The Beginning of Convenience, an entirely felted supermarket at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas.

item.title: What’s the Right Way to Honor Ana Mendieta? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
I hate the rain, but I recognize the poetic justice of a tarnished colonial commemoration through Thursday’s forecasted washout. In the era of fast fashion, data centers, and big agriculture, the world’s most precious resource will (hopefully) nourish the land while disturbing those who exploit it. It’s hard to be mad at that, even if the sensation of wet socks squelching in soaked shoes makes me want to jump out of my own skin and start orbiting earth. 

The Museum of Modern Art’s experimental arm, MoMA PS1, just announced that it’s hosting a group exhibition on Latin American art and fashion next spring. Malvestir will broach a variety of topics, including reclaiming Indigenous cosmologies and craftsmanship from the commoditized grip of Western appropriation, apparel’s role in counterculture and empowering the marginalized, and the creative, function-forward reuse of the incalculable textile waste that the United States unceremoniously dumps onto Central and South America. 

Also on the topic of land and its resources, MoMA announced its forthcoming Ana Mendieta retrospective opening in late 2027, which will focus on the late artist’s material expansion, cross-cultural infusions, and boundary-shattering interdisciplinary process in chronological fashion. Like the major exhibition that’s still on at the Tate Modern, MoMA’s retrospective also veers away from discussing Mendieta’s untimely death and the speculation surrounding it. It’s an ongoing dilemma — allowing Mendieta’s work to be displayed and contextualized outside of the implications of her tragically punctuated life is interpreted by some as prioritizing the artist’s agency and impact and message, while others regard it as a deliberate erasure of part of her story, considering the subject matter she tackled. 

I don’t know what the right call is. 

The retrospective will also unpack Mendieta’s provocative early performance art, including the confrontational interventions she staged as a reaction to the rape and murder of a fellow University of Iowa student, Sarah Ann Ottens, in 1973. The world has changed beyond recognition in the last 50 years, but the needle has merely twitched in regard to addressing and remedying misogyny and violence against women in contemporary society, as the last few months (if not the decade) would indicate. At the International Center of Photography, Spanish artist Laia Abril combs through the historic, systemic, and interpersonal bolsters of rape culture. Abril’s Black-and-white photos document the clothes worn by survivors of all ages at the time of their assault, the material culture codifying assault and kidnapping as colonial and war-related “conquests,” and other astonishingly overt examples of subjugation and dehumanization as they simultaneously evolve in contemporaneity while channeling centuries of mistreatment. 

This is some heavy stuff to ruminate on, but the much-needed dead air between marquee auctions and Miami Art Week offers some breathing room away from the market frivolity obscuring the true power of art. I hope the rain and the long weekend will give me a nice blank slate to meditate on. 

Have a safe and healthy holiday season, everyone. Travel safely, and take care.

From Our Critics

Alina Cohen

Laia Abril: On Rape and Institutional Failure at International Center of Photography

"Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage."

item.title: Iraq’s Museums Are Finally Opening Their Doors Again - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In 2022, Iraq’s National Museum in Baghdad reopened after being closed for three years following political unrest. Then in 2024, the museum closed again, this time for renovations. Now, it’s scheduled to open on December 1.

The Art Newspaper reported that the museum will open with several new galleries, such as the Abbasid and Islamic galleries. There will also be specially curated wings.

The museum will display artifacts including winged bulls (lamassu) and stone carvings depicting legendary Assyrian monarchs, ancient clay tablets and historical prisms recording legal codes, calligraphic friezes, stone carvings, glassworks, and mosaics that have been recovered and restored. According to the newspaper Iraqi News, the museum’s doors are opening to domestic visitors, international tourists, and researchers from around the world.

The reopening of the museum has been a long time coming. In 2003, the National Museum was the subject of looting during the US-led invasion. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has said that reopening the museum in December, rather than January 2027, is a priority, and that he also has plans for “a new building that befits the historical and civilizational value of Iraq.”

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum, told the Art Newspaper that the reopening of the museum “is an important moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism.”

As Iraq rebuilds itself after years of political unrest, the museums’ opening is a big step for the country’s cultural sector.

The Abbasid Palace in Baghdad opened its doors on November 15, and Iraq’s first Jewish museum, the Shamash Museum, opened its doors on October 22. Many of Iraq’s museums are also close to its large-scale monuments that are part of the city’s charm, such as the Al-Shaheed Monument designed by Iraqi sculptor Ismail Fatah al-Turk, the Monument to the Unknown Soldier designed by Khaled al-Rahal and Marcello D’Olivo, and the Saving Iraqi Culture Monument designed by Mohammed Ghani Hikmat.

item.title: After a Two-Decade Renovation, the Old Acropolis Museum Reopens - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After shuttering in 2007 to undergo a €6.2 million ($6.8 million) renovation, the Old Acropolis Museum reopened yesterday, November 23, in Athens, Greece.

Built in 1874 as Greece's first purpose-built museum, the refurbished institution is outfitted with digital displays and live conservation areas open to public view, according to the Associated Press.

The stone-clad museum is situated southeast of the Parthenon, offering an unrivaled view of the preeminent monument. When the museum closed in 2007, it was converted into an administrative building, while its previous holdings were moved to the New Acropolis Museum, which had been established over a century after its older counterpart.

item.title: Performance Artists Who Put Their Bodies on the Line - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Why do a performance art festival tied to national political issues foregrounded in the midterm election? In a moment when cultural and political institutions are retreating from provocative stances into solipsism and leisure, and government funding for the arts is but one of the many areas being slashed by right-wing political operatives, it might seem like the opposite of common sense to be opening a museum dedicated to presenting and preserving the least marketable and most controversial aspect of contemporary art: performance.

Instead, the opening of the Performance Art Museum in Los Angeles, the first US museum dedicated to this ephemeral medium, has been met with tremendous support. This is because performance, with its emphasis on embodied experience, altered psychological states, challenging social dynamics, and the absurd, provides a necessary counteraction to the dissociation and isolation of our fractured and digitized society.

Since the early 20th century, artists have deployed performance as a medium for political commentary. Dada artists in Zurich and Berlin played with the emptiness of political speech in war-torn Europe while Mavo artists in Meiji Japan used cross-dressing and shock value to mock the nation’s entanglement in colonial wars in China and Russia. With the midterm elections unfolding against a backdrop of unrelenting genocide, the embodied stakes of performance serve to sharpen its critique. The influencer news cycle has shortened our attention spans from 24 hours, already a significant shift manifested via CNN and Headline News during the Gulf War and honed during 9/11, to a far shorter, dopamine-fueled spike of rage-and-crash out that can be repeated multiple times in a single day. The war on Gaza has both numbed us to atrocities in our feed, and disconnected us from our own bodies and communities as we quietly absorb the unspoken impacts of the violence that we outsource. 

In the 1960s and 1970s, this absorbed violence erupted in the work of the Actionist artists including Hermann Nitsch, Rudolf Schwarzkogler, Valie Export, and Gina Pane. High Performance magazine was the first outlet to cover these artists in the United States and an emerging generation of artists informed by them, including Chris Burden and Kim Jones, who took significant physical risks in performances that openly critiqued the prolonged war in Vietnam. At the same time, the sexual revolution was underway and artists including Barbara T. Smith, Suzanne Lacy, and Johanna Went put their bodies on the line accordingly, looking at the pleasures and the risks of erotic life from feminist perspectives. Artist and poet Sue Dakin, the publisher of High Performance, ran a campaign for president as an independent candidate in 1984.

These histories inform the two-year Performance Art Museum initiative, High Performance: A 2 Year Conference for which my colleague Leon J. Hilton and I organized Public Spirits: A Performance Art Festival on October 23, 2026. 

Emerging out of these practices and the magazine’s coverage of them, the 1980 Public Spirit festival, organized by the Highland Art Agents (including Paul McCarthy, Barbara T. Smith, Chip Chapman, John Duncan, and High Performance editor Linda Frye Burnham) through LACE, LA’s longest-running experimental art space, featured 60 artists and over 100 performances over two weeks in May and four weeks in October. Many of the works were staged in rooms at the American Hotel and were intimate in scale. Some, like the Feminist Art Workers’ Bill of Rights advocating for the ill-fated Equal Rights Amendment or The Waitresses’ Coffee Cauldron honoring women in service work, were explicitly political in nature. Many followed participant Allan Kaprow’s model for Happenings, being unscripted actions that turned absurd, comedic, or disturbing. Some involved singing, dancing, or traditional theatrical presentations — including a musical by Carole Caroompas about unreliable exes, a dance number by Nancy Buchanan about covert US intervention in Central America, and a play by Alexis Smith and Heidi Hardin titled “Stardust” that featured an unknown Whoopi Goldberg. A gallery at LACE was designated the “Public Spirit Remnants Room” and exhibited artifacts from the performances after the fact. 

The election in November 1980 marked the ascent of Ronald Reagan to the presidency, bringing the era of government funding that enabled Public Spirit to a close. 1980 was the peak year for funding for artists through the Comprehensive Employment and Training Act (CETA) passed under Richard Nixon, and for alternative spaces through the National Endowment for the Arts. Resources are more scarce and costs are much higher for artists working today. A performance festival on this scale that would be impactful both for audiences and for the participating artists would be inconceivable with the capacity that the 1980 Public Spirit organizers were able to muster. Our 2026 homage was more modest in scale with four artists highlighted over a single day at our home base, the Performance Building in Chinatown, and nearby locations at the Los Angeles State Historic Park and Homeboy Art Academy. Our artists — Pau S. Pescador, Jade Guanaro Kuriki-Olivo (Puppies Puppies), Da Ron Vinson, and Ryat Yezbick — balanced poetics with politics to address hot-button issues at the top of this election cycle such as AI and mass surveillance, transgender civil rights, sexual exploitation and trafficking in corridors of power, racial profiling, and gender discrimination. Our intention was to build connections within our new neighborhood and to bring our community of artists and supporters together with the public in a way that felt provocative but also physically and emotionally safe for vulnerable populations. 

Despite the bleak political landscape, we hoped to generate collective joy through demonstrations of resistance. Politics in 2026 can be discouraging at best, at worst a bloodbath of allegations and backbiting. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar last month as a political stunt. Outgoing Michigan Representative Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers rather than her own party’s candidate for the US Senate, Abdul Al-Sayed, was a peak act of political theater designed to prolong a losing candidate’s influence when the reins of actual power have slipped from her grasp. The sitting president resorts to theatrics on a daily basis to distract from the incompetence of his governance. Much of our political culture today consists of symbolic gestures, a stunt politics based on the cynical expectation that nothing real is at stake. Yet the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids and mass shootings have real long-term consequences that quickly slip from the headlines, replaced by another circus act.

The right, with its relentless homoerotic homophobia, is a parody of itself. Yesterday obsessed with Hasan Piker’s shirtless photos, today with Long Island congressional candidate Chris Gallant’s decades-old BDSM modeling spread for gay San Francisco landmark, Mr. S. Leather. Until recently, the response from the Democrats would be to fan the moral panic, undermining their own candidates’ strong policy records with ruminations about their private lives. As Gallant notes, though he lost his race, he demonstrated that the bar for personal behavior has dropped so low under the current administration and the level of hypocrisy grown so high that nothing he has done or could do as a gay person in a consensual adult context ought to be viewed as invalidating to his political career. Anxiety about the body, gender, and sexuality drives productivity, with relentless labor framed as the only alternative to a life of exploitation, and catastrophic debt the only route to sexual desirability. The performance artist seizes control of these narratives of the social body, often leaning into the worst possible interpretation to highlight the absurdity of the whole proposition.

In inviting me to write this opinion piece, Hyperallergic’s Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara asked me point-blank: “Aren’t all politicians really performance artists?” To which I say yes, but not in the ways that matter. A real performance artist puts their body on the line, asking of themselves more than they would ever ask of another. Zohran Mamdani jumping fully clothed into a swimming pool is political theater, but he is no more a performance artist than his idol, Fiorello La Guardia — a great orator who built a cult of personality, yes, but fundamentally a legal and economic reformer. The theater is a tool to get popular buy-in for necessarily dry bureaucratic actions. Incoming New York Representative Brad Lander getting arrested in Palestine is theater that points to a bureaucratic inequality. His passport and his privilege get him released within 24 hours while Arab activists sit in jail on equally bogus charges. 

The performance artist does not have an easily readable political agenda. She seeks something more ephemeral and simultaneously more real — metempsychosis — achieving total transformation by killing the Ego if not the physical body. The performance artist attempts to close the gap between their privilege and the suffering of others by getting down to the level of the least of us. It is not religion, but it is a ritual of transubstantiation. Perhaps Gallant, with his Avatar: The Last Airbender haircut and his U.S. Army and Fire Department bona fides, would be the closest a politician has come recently to putting some real skin in the game. 

Politics, however altruistic, elevates the self. Performance art annihilates and remakes it, refracting into the audience through the prism of the artist. Politics changes the system, but performance art changes the artist and the viewer by foregrounding and renegotiating the social contract. Politics can only work with what we see. Performance engages what we can’t.

item.title: A Minimalist, a Maximalist, and 30 Years of Friendship - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Two person shows are taking over the art world, with galleries doubling as matchmakers, mostly pairing dead artists with market darlings. But of course, nothing beats conversation between two old friends.

At Gladstone in New York this fall, that’s just what you’ll get, with a new show from British artists Sarah Lucas and Cerith Wyn Evans titled “Je Pense.”

The two talked to Art in America about the exhibition, and their 30-year friendship, below.

You two have been friends since the ’90s. How’d you meet?

Cerith Wyn Evans: I never can answer questions like that because I never remember. We were probably both drunk somewhere.

Sarah Lucas: It’s tricky.

CWE: I do remember hearing of you. I was close with a painter at the time, Angus Cook, and I’d ask him things like “What’s Gary Hume like?,” all this kind of stuff. Later I quipped, “We should really be talking about his girlfriend, a much better artist. She’s called Sarah Lucas.”

Angus said he had met you once: He knocked on the door and you answered—allegedly!—and he said “Hi, are you Gary?” and you replied “NO.” He told me “Oh my God, She’s incredible!”

SL: I remember meeting Angus at a party Matthew Marks gave for Gary, maybe that’s where I met you. A lot of things were happening at that time, around 1990; something was burgeoning. I met a lot of people then that became friends for life.

CWE: There was a mileuuuu.

You can’t make new old friends! When I saw that you two were showing together, I admit my first thought was: a minimalist and a maximalist walk into a bar.

CWE: Who’s who? [laughs] I’m certainly the maximalist.

Ha. All that’s to say, at first glance, I thought of you two as having quite different sensibilities, but they really do converge beautifully in the gallery. I know you’ve wanted to show together for quite a while.

SL: We’ve kicked the notion around for a long time, but it was more of a mythic show, something we might do some day—it wasn’t about whether we ever did it or not.

CWE: I think if you really really care how another person thinks, if you don’t take them for granted, you imagine your dialogue… but also the distance between our work allows a certain level of respect. Nancy Spector invited us, and really, the show’s a kind of hologram that Nancy has somehow… well, she’s the Wizard of Oz.

So the differences help. Okay, I have to ask about the burnt-out car in the gallery, obviously.

CWE: For me, that’s the fulcrum of the entire exhibition because it’s so brutal. It’s like a black hole in the middle of the entire thing, and a vortex that everything sucks everything else in, or spits it all out, or something. It’s phenomenal, extraordinary and also this quotidian tragedy, a very pure readymade. Sarah bought it at an auction, already burnt. I guess weird death perverts buy these things.

SL: I have no idea who would buy these things… apart from us.

Did you make the work in tandem and plan it out, or just bring things together at the end? I love how Sarah’s sculpture makes Cerith’s tower feel very phallic.

CWE: No, we’ve just always been very erotic, very horny. See, this is the maximalist in me coming out.

SL: Besides, things are always different when you get them somewhere anyway.

Have you guys been like doing studio visits and giving each other feedback over the years?

CWE: No no no. It’s organic. It’s natural. It’s spiritual. We’re not really that organized.

SL: That’s probably why we like each other. We get on because we don’t have that kind of mindset that would make us, I don’t know, strategic.

I’m just thinking about a lot of younger artists who are working hard to sustain creative community. I don’t know if you have thoughts or advice for them.

SL: No one takes advice, do they? Though I will say, younger artists should be in more group shows. When you’re young, you’re so eager to have your moment in the spotlight.

Has your friendship ever felt competitive?

SL: We just aren’t really strategic like that. I’m not a jealous person by nature. I’m just in my own world, making work.

CWE: I think it’s sad when people compare themselves and are concerned with who’s more famous or younger or richer.

Do you talk about art together then, or other stuff?

SL: Never.

CWE: I don’t think I talk about anything else. But it depends what how you by mean “Art.” I’m obsessed by creativity more than much art with a price tag.

SL: That’s true, art can be anything.

item.title: Jessica Craig-Martin’s Exercise in Name-Dropping - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The central, perplexing conundrum of the “nepo baby” arguably is this: Does the nepo baby possess talent, and is that talent to any degree independent of the considerable social and financial benefits bestowed upon said nepo baby from birth?

In I Regret I Am Able To Attend: A Life Among Artists (2026), photographer Jessica Craig-Martin, daughter of Irish painter Michael Craig-Martin and Jan Hashey (sometime artist but more successful real estate broker), chooses to quote Paul Auster, a giant of 20th-century American literature, in the introduction to her memoir: “Stories only happen to those who tell them.” The quote is meant to underline her insistence that this book is not a memoir, nor a narrative, only a collection of tales, thereby excusing any requirement for fact-checking or referencing, despite it very clearly being an exhaustive narrative of her life and that of her parents. The choice of quote also underlines the book’s tone: These stories are remarkable because of who they happened to, regardless of whether they are actually interesting or not. And that is how celebrity — the condition of being famous simply for being famous — works. 

Craig-Martin weaves her parents’ experiences into her own, with several chapters throughout returning entirely to their lives as side quests, detailing which houses they bought and how they were decorated and who their friends were and how much money they earned, variously bouncing between London and New York and dragging the author between them. Where there is an excess of material and social detail, however — the name-dropping comes in lists — there is a mystifying sense of disengagement or interest in her parents’ own artistic enterprises. We are told what Michael did and what accolades he received but nothing substantial about Craig-Martin’s emotional or intellectual connection to his work. Her tonal detachment at attending, say, the first-ever performance of Gilbert George’s “The Singing Sculpture” (1969) cleaves a divide between her, dragged to the debut as par for the course of a daughter of a well-connected artist, and us, mortals who would have killed to witness this legendary moment in art history. What is present from the start is a keen eye for fashion, even if it is delivered via observations about how her mother was painfully more chic than the other parents picking their kids up from school.

item.title: The Inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards Highlight the Vagaries of Daily Life - Colossal
item.description:
From architecture to brooding skies to happenstance, the images of the finalists of the inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards highlight the humor, friction, and tenderness of everyday moments. The competition is presented by AUSSIE STREET, an organization founded by street photographers to showcase work from across the nation, which builds upon a series of festivals presented between 2018 and 2023.

Co-founder Sam Ferris says that the outfit’s mission is to not only exhibit great photos but to tap into the dispersed network of those who make them. “Street photography can be a pretty solitary obsession,” he says in a statement. “But there’s a whole community of people out there doing exactly the same thing. Getting them together, seeing the work printed, and hearing the stories behind the photographs is a reminder that we’re part of something much bigger than our individual pursuits.”

The awards opened with a show of 25 finalists at Studio 551 in Newtown, New South Wales, and AUSSIE STREET awarded the top prize to Adam Oxley. “One of the things I love about street photography is that you don’t need an enormous budget to make a remarkable image,” Ferris adds. “You need curiosity, patience, persistence and a way of seeing. Some of the most extraordinary photographs happen in completely ordinary places.”

See more on AUSSIE STREET’s Instagram, where you can keep an eye out for updates about the 2027 edition.

item.title: Joni Mitchell Has Some News - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In her song “A Case of You,” Joni Mitchell described herself as “a lonely painter / I live in a box of paints.” She has never been a particularly shy one. The famously elusive artist, who has pronounced painting her "first love" before music, makes plain statements in NEWS, a collection of political paintings.

Conceived and designed by Mitchell, the book unfurls a scathing rebuke of recent Republican administrations in the United States. Twenty-three paintings are presented chronologically, with a handful created between 2001 and 2004 and the majority made in the last 18 months. Works from the Bush years show the Twin Towers aflame with a sinister face in the smoke or a bare-chested blonde woman who sits astride Osama Bin Laden’s shoulders.

More recent works feature Adolf Hitler with the letters "MGGA" ("Make Germany Great Again"), former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem on horseback labeled “grifter,” and a triptych of Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, and President Trump as disgraced royalty playing cards. A spread of all the works becomes a Thunderdome-like arena of modern US politics — ending with a self-portrait of Mitchell receiving a Kennedy Center Honor. As if the answer to all that chaos is elevating impactful art.

item.title: Objects, Landscapes and Other Unique Histories - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
An artificial plant, a fragment of upholstery and a stretch of reclaimed coastline might seem unlikely subjects for a discussion about how we understand the world. However, each carries a history that extends beyond its immediate appearance. Objects are shaped by the circumstances of their production and use; landscapes bear the consequences of development. For artists Nabuqi and Karimah Ashadu, these traces provide a way of examining the relationship between physical surroundings and lived experience. Their forthcoming exhibitions, Hidden Breeze and RUSHES, approach this territory through sculpture, installation, film and painting, bringing questions of perception, labour and value into a compelling dialogue.

Although their practices emerge from different cultural and philosophical contexts, both artists pay close attention to the meanings accumulated by ordinary things. Beijing-based Nabuqi explores how objects influence perception, drawing on phenomenology and the philosophical writings of Martin Heidegger. Ashadu, a British-born Nigerian artist, investigates labour, masculinity and economic inequality through the experiences of people living and working in Nigeria. Their approaches intersect around an interest in the relationship between material form and human experience. Where Nabuqi unsettles the familiar appearance of objects, Ashadu examines the histories and social conditions that determine their use.

Opening on 25 November, Hidden Breeze marks Nabuqi’s first solo exhibition with Sadie Coles HQ, 10 years after her participation in Zhongguo 2185, curated by Victor Wang. Her sculptures and installations frequently draw on recognisable forms, introducing subtle alterations that challenge the assumptions attached to everyday objects. At the Kingly Street Gallery, curtains establish an environment organised around wind, water and plant life, creating a landscape through which visitors encounter artificial and organic forms. Rotating knots, titled The Motionless, suggest air currents through their suspended configurations, while a waterfall appears as a static image hanging on the wall.

Artificiality becomes particularly apparent in The Question-Posing, where familiar plastic office plants are recast as botanical specimens in aluminium, painted in vivid shades of green, red and black. Their arrangement within architectural structures recalls the presentation of objects in scientific collections, although their manufactured origins complicate the authority of such classification. Nabuqi draws attention to the ways in which appearances influence our understanding of what is natural, authentic or functional. In The Slightly Swaying, a monumental tree-like sculpture composed of stacked bronze discs can be rotated, introducing movement into a form associated with permanence. Its weight contrasts with the delicate suggestion of swaying branches, giving the sculpture a physical and conceptual tension.

Nabuqi’s investigation of objects has interesting parallels with Otobong Nkanga, whose multidisciplinary practice examines the relationships between natural resources, extraction and global trade. Nkanga frequently traces the journeys of materials through different geographical and economic systems, revealing the human histories concealed within seemingly ordinary substances. Her work offers a useful counterpoint to Nabuqi’s philosophical enquiry: both artists ask viewers to reconsider what an object represents, although Nkanga places greater emphasis on its ecological and political history. Mona Hatoum provides another perspective through sculptures that transform domestic objects into unsettling encounters, exposing the fragility of familiar environments. Together, these practices demonstrate the continuing importance of sculpture as a means of questioning how objects acquire meaning.

Labour and the histories of everyday materials take centre stage in Ashadu’s RUSHES, opening on 2 December at the gallery’s Savile Row space. The exhibition presents WAVES (2026), her latest film, in the UK for the first time, following its European premiere at Kestner Gesellschaft in Hanover. Set in Lagos’s Oniru District, the film follows men working at an informal carwash on a narrow strip of land recently reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean. As they wash vehicles, conversations reveal their ambitions, personal histories and reasons for migrating to the city. Recounted in Hausa, a widely spoken language in Northern Nigeria, their accounts establish a portrait of individuals negotiating the demands of working life.

The ocean provides a striking visual counterpoint to their circumstances. Its vastness suggests abundance, yet the men have limited access to the water surrounding them, exposing an uncomfortable contradiction between natural resources and their distribution. Images of foaming waves unfold alongside the repetitive gestures of washing, while the seawall behind the workers marks a landscape shaped by reclamation and development. The film recalls the environmental concerns explored by Zina Saro-Wiwa, whose moving-image practice has examined identity, ecological change and the legacy of oil extraction in the Niger Delta. Both artists consider how economic interests transform landscapes and affect the communities that inhabit them. Ashadu, however, keeps her focus closely on individual experience, allowing the men’s voices to convey the complexity of their circumstances without reducing their lives to illustrations of inequality.

The film’s concerns extend into a series of paintings on moulded carpet panels and new works on paper presented across the gallery’s upper floor. The upholstery used in the paintings has been extracted from minivans like those appearing in WAVES, retaining the contours, marks and apertures of its previous life. Ashadu describes this circulation of materials as circular trade, a process through which objects move between contexts and acquire new forms of value. Their transformation from vehicle interiors into painted surfaces brings the history of their use into the exhibition. The material itself becomes a record of movement, connecting the film’s observations of everyday labour with the circulation of commodities.

Masculinity emerges as another significant subject in the works on paper. Men appear beneath blue skies and billowing clouds, while other compositions place them against rose-tinted sunsets, dressed in faux-designer clothing. These details reveal how fashion and consumer culture contribute to the construction of masculine identity, providing ways to express aspiration and establish social recognition. Ashadu is attentive to the emotional significance of these gestures, particularly within circumstances where economic opportunity remains unevenly distributed. Her depictions hold desire and vulnerability in close proximity, giving the men an individuality that extends beyond their working lives. The result is a nuanced examination of how appearance, labour and self-worth intersect.

Ashadu’s movement between documentary film and physical materials raises questions about how working lives are represented and who controls the images through which they become visible. Hito Steyerl’s investigations into the circulation of images offer a broader theoretical context, particularly her examination of the political and economic systems that shape contemporary visual culture. Ashadu approaches these concerns through a more intimate engagement with particular people and places, allowing the material conditions of life to inform the work. Her paintings extend the film’s observations, giving objects a presence that carries their previous use into the gallery. Film, painting and sculpture consequently become interconnected ways of examining how images and materials acquire meaning.

Presented within the same gallery programme, Hidden Breeze and RUSHES offer distinct perspectives on the relationship between objects and the lives that surround them. Nabuqi’s installations invite visitors to question the reliability of appearances, while Ashadu traces the economic and personal histories embedded in landscapes, commodities and working bodies. Their differing approaches demonstrate the breadth of contemporary artistic enquiry, from questions about perception to investigations of labour, migration and social identity. An artificial plant and a fragment of minivan upholstery become revealing in this context: both carry meanings that exceed their original functions. What remains visible is only part of their story; the rest resides in the histories, movements and human experiences that have shaped them.

Nabuqi: Hidden Breeze is at Sadie Coles HQ, London from 25 November – 20 February.

Karimah Ashadu: RUSHES is at Sadie Coles HQ, London from 2 December – 27 February.

Find out more: sadiecoles.com

Words: Shirley Stevenson

item.title: Miami Through the GTA VI Looking-Glass - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Days before the Venice Biennale opened, the Golden Lion jury resigned amid calls to exclude Israel from the festival. Dozens of artists and pavilions took themselves out of the running in solidarity. Now, as the exhibition draws to a close, the Biennale is ready to present its visitors’ choice awards — a “poisoned chalice,” in the words of the Art Not Genocide Alliance (ANGA), that “few want to win.” ANGA reflects on a historic year of organizing against attempts to artwash Israel’s assault on Palestine in an opinion piece today.

As gamers everywhere pore over Grand Theft Auto VI, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia sits down with Miami-based artists misael soto and Leo Castañeda to make sense of the game’s many tensions and complexities, while Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar tracks down its various art references. In another form of uncanny valley, Associate Editor Phillip Pyle wanders through empty corporate offices in Midtown Manhattan, transformed by artists who dismantle the systems of technocracy from the inside out. More to start your week below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

The Venice Biennale’s Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. | Art Not Genocide Alliance

item.title: Inside Edward Said’s World - Hyperallergic
item.description:
‘Tis the season for great documentaries. Twenty years after the death of Palestinian literary critic and theorist Edward Said, a new film revisits his life and legacy. Moustafa Bayoumi, a student of Said himself, posits that it offers a new generation a glimpse of Said’s indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight. 

The lovely Eileen G’Sell takes a look at Trisha Ziff’s latest documentary, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, which screened recently at DOC NYC. The film considers the commercial afterlife of Frida Kahlo, asking how the artist’s personal history has been whitewashed even as her image circulates endlessly through retail culture. What happens when an artist’s legacy becomes as much a consumer product as a creative one?

And finally, if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, what are you waiting for? It may be the best film I’ve seen all year, full of unexpected twists, turns, and glorious awkward pauses. Though billed as a documentary, the film raises what I think is a more intriguing question: Is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian? Not to toot my own horn, but I explore that possibility and more in my recent review, though be warned: spoilers abound.

—Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor

Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise

As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? | Rebecca Schiffman

item.title: Lucy Sante Talks About What Collage Enables That Writing Can’t - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Lucy Sante started making collages long before she established herself as a writer of incisive theories of photography (see Walker Evans, from 1999, Evidence, from 1992, and 2009’s Folk Photography: The American Real-Photo Postcard 1905–1930); of urban studies (see Low Life: Lures and Snares of Old New York, her 1991 chronicle of the city’s underworlds); and of personal history (2024’s I Heard Her Call My Name: A Memoir of Transition). As a teenage émigré in the 1960s, she would clip and assemble images from magazines, a practice she has continued on and off ever since—drawing lasting inspiration from the metaphysical juxtapositions of René Magritte, a fellow Belgian. As a clerk at the Strand, a storied used bookshop in New York, she began working with a wider range of materials, from cast-off paperbacks and technical manuals to medical textbooks and other arcane publications. All the while, she developed a mysterious and poetic style of collage that mixed imagery from different eras and suggested the outlines of stories, however elusive those might be.

Over the decades, Sante devoted herself most fervently to writing, with a focus on photography: In 2023, she retired as a professor of writing and the history of photography at Bard College. Her newest book, My Heart & I Agree (2026), is an essay collection that covers subjects including Surrealist photography, cowboy iconography, and Soul Train. There, her keen eye toward camera culture remains evident. She refocused some of her energies on collage in recent years, and her visual work featured this past spring in solo exhibitions at Picture Theory in Chelsea and at the American Academy of Arts and Letters in upper Manhattan, where an early collage from the ’70s joined works made since 2020. From her home in upstate New York, Sante spoke with A.i.A. about learning to look through magazines, moving her way into fine-art collage, and finding poetry in images she gives new life.

What do you remember about your early collages that made you want to keep making them?

I had two sources of materials for my earliest collages: a stack of Arizona Highways magazines from the 1950s and early ’60s, and my parents’ subscription to Life. I remember a collage that I made featuring Jimi Hendrix and a mushroom cloud: That was hip. I was imitating collages I saw—not artistic collages, but collages in popular media. In the early Rolling Stone, on the letters page, almost every week they’d have a collage by this graphic designer named Wilfried Sätty, whose house I stayed in years later, after his death in 1982. He had a particular style: outer space plus old engravings.

Had you made other kinds of visual art?

I’m colorblind, and that was a big problem for me. I drew, but had to work in black and white. I wasn’t that bad—just not as good as I wanted to be. In high school, I started making band flyers, which I continued when I was living on the Lower East Side in the 1970s and ’80s. I made several for the Del-Byzanteens, a band I also wrote lyrics for. Many people in the band became celebrated in one way or another: Jim Jarmusch as a filmmaker, Jamie Nares as a painter, and Phil Kline as a composer.

How did your work at the Strand Bookstore find its way into your collages?

We started a collective publication called Stranded that was originally going to be like a workers’ gripe sheet. But instead, we published art and poetry and stuff like that. I had collage-like things in all four issues. Within a week of my starting, Fred Bass [fabled owner of the Strand] named me the paperback department—I was the entire department all by myself. Bookmen in that period did not take paperbacks seriously and just put them out in the 25-cent carts. That meant I had to deal with romance books, and when I put those out on Thursdays, they were mobbed by old ladies, and it was a nightmare. But it also meant that whenever they bought a library, they would throw me everything that wasn’t a hardcover book, including magazines, maps, postcards, and all kinds of stuff that I took home and still have. I made collages recently with material I acquired back then at the Strand.

What was the Strand like as a downtown institution then compared to now?

Nobody was very literary on the Lower East Side in the ’70s. People were starting bands and making movies. There wasn’t even painting at the time. We had to wait for Basquiat. In the ’70s, we had some bad poets, a few bad essayists. Nobody [in the neighborhood] wrote fiction. But at that point, the sociology was nothing to compare to now, because you could waltz into New York City hitchhiking from Denver or somewhere and find yourself a cheap apartment and get a job at the Strand. Your salary would pay your rent, and you had money left over to go clubbing. That’s long gone now.

What were you looking for? What made something conducive to collage?

I liked texture and was really interested in contrasting eras. I liked faded color. I was taking inspiration from a lot of different sources. Of the flyers I made for the Del-Byzanteens, one of them [drew from] big posters that a syndicate put out to try to promote a science-fiction comic strip. I X-Acto–knifed out the thought balloons and filled them in with other material. That was because I had a friend who’d just come over from Paris with a Situationist International book, and I got inspired by that.

You mentioned beginning with an interest in popular-media collage. What art world collagists interested you later on?

I was inspired by Max Ernst and Robert Rauschenberg. I found a book by Jess, Robert Duncan’s partner and a great collage artist. I discovered Bruce Conner and, of course, the Surrealists and Dadaists—Berlin Dada, especially, with John Heartfield and Hannah Höch. And the Russians, like El Lissitzky and Alexander Rodchenko. There’s a whole world of collage out there.

How would you describe your decision-making process?

There are collages that I don’t quite know how to resolve. They might need something else, but I don’t know what. Often they’re just made on the spot.

One work that especially caught my eye in your Arts and Letters show was De La (2023). How did you arrive upon the composition for that?

That’s my favorite work of mine. That’s one I’m keeping. It just came together in a particular way, and it zinged. And I can take you through exactly how I made it, because I do remember. The materials go back to 1981, which was the tail end of people selling shit on the street on the Lower East Side. There had been this kind of ad hoc 24/7 flea market around Astor Place. One night, I was walking down St. Marks Place, and there was a guy selling damaged posters. I bought a shopping bag’s worth for 10 bucks; they were all falling to pieces. The yellow and white in De La is from a poster for an early movie by the Italian director Elio Petri, and the lettering comes from miscellaneous papers from a local auction up here [in upstate New York]. It had all kinds of crap, including a poster for a touring Laurel and Hardy anthology film in Spanish. The tire at the top comes from a French car magazine from the ’30s, and the chrysanthemum comes from a seed-company ad in Life. The glove is from a 1950s Punch, a humor magazine that had wonderful advertising. And then the star of the show is the woman with the fingerprints on her back, which I’d been saving up for the longest time. It comes from a French soft-porn magazine from the ’30s. It was magic how they all came together.

What do letters and different bits of text do for you in collage work?

There’s lettering in, I’d say, 95 percent of my collages, and that’s partly because I kind of think of them as movie posters. One of my original inspirations was the posters I saw when I first started going to the movies as a child, for films like Ben Hur (1959) and Hawaii (1966). They had enormous, sculpted letters for the title, and then there would be little figures swirling around them illustrating the scope of the story. In a way, everything I do refers back to those.

Are there writerly aspects to the collage-making process for you? They can’t help but suggest some sort of narrative for the viewer, but I don’t know about the maker, necessarily…

It’s ambiguity central. I started life, so to speak, as a poet. I later realized I was a prose writer, but poetry is at the heart of everything for me. Among other things, that means making a structure from a sort of lean-to of ambiguities—one ambiguity resting on another, all suggesting a story and all suggesting a meaning but never actually giving it to you. If I make a collage and it seems to have a legible message, I have failed.

What makes you turn to collage instead of writing when a creative impulse strikes?

It’s something I feel in my hands—like, “By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked this way comes.” It’s the feeling that I need to make something. Being a writer does not involve the body the way that making visual art does, and I have that craving. I wanted to be an artist before I ever thought of being a writer.

Because I have so much to do right now, I’m not running down to the basement to make more collages. But in the meantime, I’ve bought things on eBay. I bought a bunch of 19th-century chromolithographs I’m eager to use, and somebody sold me these incredibly dirty comics—I don’t mean dirty like sexy, but dirty like they were lying in a crawl space for 75 years. I like dirt. I like fading. I like things that are crinkled, things that are ripped. I prefer things that are damaged, because they carry their histories. They establish a custodial chain and have a lot of dead people’s fingerprints on them. If something looks like it comes out of the box, even if it was published in 1922, I’m far less interested than if it’s fucked up.

item.title: Random International and the Question of Artificial Life - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
What happens when a machine begins to look back? As artificial intelligence moves beyond the screen and into physical space, the distinction between human presence and technological simulation becomes increasingly difficult to sustain. Contemporary artists are interrogating this boundary through responsive environments, generative systems and embodied interfaces, questioning the assumptions through which intelligence, consciousness and agency are defined. However, a machine’s capacity to register and respond to human behaviour does not necessarily mean that it understands what it encounters. The gap between perception and comprehension lies at the heart of Random International’s In all chaos there is a cosmos, presented with HOFA.io at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026 as part of Generation, the latest edition of Zero 10.

Curated by Karen Archey with Eli Scheinman, Generation considers how emerging technologies are reshaping artistic practice and the conditions in which art is produced and experienced. Its subject is particularly urgent at a moment when artificial intelligence is increasingly described as collaborator, tool and potential autonomous agent, often with little distinction between computational capability and consciousness. Random International approaches these questions through ambiguity. The London-based studio creates situations in which viewers become conscious of their own tendency to attribute intention to responsive forms. What appears to be an encounter with an independent intelligence becomes an examination of the expectations through which human beings recognise agency.

Donna Haraway’s writing on the cyborg offers a useful framework for understanding this instability, particularly her challenge to fixed distinctions between human and machine. In A Cyborg Manifesto, the cyborg unsettles the boundaries through which identity and subjectivity are conventionally organised, proposing hybrid forms that resist familiar categories. Random International’s sculptures do not simply illustrate this proposition; they bring its implications into physical space. Human figures emerge through computational processes, while their behaviour is shaped by the presence and movement of viewers. The resulting encounter complicates the separation between observer and observed: visitors approach the work expecting to look at a representation, only to find themselves implicated in its appearance.

At the centre of the installation, a sprawling ribbon of LEDs gives form to a life-sized human figure. Camera tracking and machine-learning processes enable the sculpture to register its surroundings, producing a responsive presence that appears to move between recognition and abstraction. Neither a conventional digital portrait nor a simulation of a person, the figure occupies an uncertain territory between representation and behaviour. Its body is distributed across light, fragmented by the structure through which it is rendered, and reconstituted through interaction. Although viewers may recognise a human presence, its apparent autonomy remains inseparable from the computational system that generates it.

Machine perception, however, should not be mistaken for consciousness. The former describes the processing and interpretation of information; the latter implies subjective experience, an awareness of being and encountering the world. One does not establish the other, however convincing a system’s responses may appear. Random International’s sculptures do not claim to establish consciousness within their computational structures; instead, they expose the assumptions through which viewers recognise agency, often attributing intention to forms that reproduce familiar patterns of behaviour. A figure that appears attentive can prompt an emotional response even when there is no evidence of an interior life behind its gestures. Much of the meaning, therefore, is supplied by the viewer, who reads recognition, curiosity or intention into a system whose operations remain computational.

Elsewhere in the installation, the human figure assumes a more controlled form. Close To Me / I and Close To Me / II translate the body into half-scale forms composed from precise LED grids. Their regular structures evoke the pixel, the basic unit through which digital images are assembled and circulated. Yet the figures also suggest a tension between the apparent freedom of the body and the systems that seek to contain, measure and reproduce it. Where the central sculpture disperses the figure across a sprawling field of light, these works retain the discipline of the grid. Their formal contrast raises a question about representation itself: can the human body ever be separated from the technologies through which it is made visible?

Light itself becomes central to the studio’s understanding of collective intelligence. Random International describes it as a medium through which individual elements produce complex and responsive wholes, an idea that gives the works a conceptual dimension beyond their technological construction. LED components matter through the relationships that allow a larger form to emerge. The resulting structures resonate with debates around distributed and non-human intelligence, while resisting the assumption that intelligence must resemble individual human thought. Complexity may arise through interaction, the sculptures suggest, although collective behaviour should not be confused with conscious experience.

The questions explored here have shaped Random International’s practice since its founding in 2005 by Hannes Koch and Florian Ortkrass. Works such as Audience (2008) and Rain Room (2012) established the studio’s interest in situations that appear to respond to the presence of visitors. In Rain Room, the experience of moving through falling water without becoming wet turns the visitor into an active participant in a technologically controlled environment. Its effect depends on a negotiation between movement and an invisible system, making the mechanics of interaction felt. Across these projects, technology is not a neutral medium but a condition through which human behaviour becomes perceptible.

The origins of these fragmented bodies can be traced to the Future Self series, developed from 2012 onwards, which explored digital representation and bodily presence. Collaborations with choreographer Wayne McGregor and composer Max Richter have extended the studio’s engagement with movement, perception and the relationship between technological systems and expression. Such intersections matter because they place computational processes in dialogue with disciplines concerned with the body as a site of knowledge. Dance, music and sculpture each offer ways of understanding experience that cannot be reduced to information alone. Random International returns to a persistent tension: what happens when systems designed to register human behaviour begin to shape how that behaviour is experienced?

As machine-learning systems enter everyday environments, the language surrounding artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly consequential. Descriptions of processing frequently slide into claims of understanding, while prediction is mistaken for intention. These shifts are not merely semantic; they influence how authority, responsibility and agency are assigned to technologies. Art can make such assumptions visible by slowing down encounters that elsewhere are automated and difficult to scrutinise. Random International does not resolve whether machines might one day possess consciousness. Instead, the work draws attention to the ease with which human observers interpret responsiveness as evidence of an inner life, revealing how much of the apparent encounter is produced by their own expectations.

In all chaos there is a cosmos forms part of Zero 10’s broader effort to consider digital and technology-led practices within contemporary art. HOFA.io’s involvement brings the installation into contact with a platform operating across digital art and Web3, placing questions of technological authorship alongside those of perception and embodiment. Yet, the work’s most compelling proposition extends beyond its relationship to a particular technological market. Its force lies in the uncertainty produced when a familiar human form appears to act beyond the viewer’s control. The sculptures may seem to recognise us, but recognition is not the same as understanding. Their most unsettling effect is to expose a distinctly human desire: to find another consciousness looking back, even when there may be nobody there.

Life in a Different Resolution is at Art Basel Miami Beach 2 – 6 December: random-international.com

Words: Simon Cartwright

item.title: Nature Up Close: From the Aesthetica Archives - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Plants and photography share a profound history, from Anna Atkins’ 19th-century cyanotypes to the modernist precision of Karl Blossfeldt. Today, a new generation of lens-based artists is dedicated to capturing the raw beauty of the natural world, often employing layers and subtle effects to craft striking, evocative imagery. This feature presents a selection of photographers previously featured in Aesthetica who transform everyday elements like flowers and leaves into something that makes us stop and look again. By setting vibrant blooms and delicate foliage against deep, dark backgrounds, these artists are led by the intensity of colour. The result is a celebration of the vibrancy inherent in nature, inviting viewers to look closer at the intricate textures and fragile beauty of our environment.

Henri Blommers

Amsterdam-based fine art photographer Henri Blommers experiments with a variety of techniques: cooking film in plant material, spraying it with agricultural chemicals or soaking negatives in salt for weeks. Blommers’ images are socially and ecologically engaged, exploring pressing topics like plastic pollution, rising sea levels or species under threat. He says, “After my divorce, I had no home and was stuck in my garden. I started growing plants and vegetables from seeds. Although I had photographed flowers all my life, it only then dawned on me that I could make my garden the starting point of something new.” 

henriblommers.com | @henriblommer

Marine Lanier

Marine Lanier (b. 1981), spent time at The Lautaret Garden in France – one of Europe’s highest-altitude botanical gardens – alongside ecologists, gardeners and scientists, where she developed large-scale images of its flora. The result is Le Jardin d’Hannibal – so named for the epic tales of Hannibal, said to have crossed the Lautaret pass during his campaign against Rome. Lanier’s pictures recall the works of Anna Atkins and Karl Blossfeldt, whilst establishing a phantasmagorical aesthetic – led by colour, light and shadow – all her own. The artist captures vegetation at nightfall, as well as minerals which glitter under the blazing sun. 

@marinelanier

Debora Lombardi

Debora Lombardi is an architect and visual designer using modern techniques to make her mark on the botanical photography genre. The detail-rich work uses the technique of ultraviolet-induced visible fluorescence to reveal pigments hidden within flowers, which emit a mesmerising glow when under UV light. Dandelions, daisies and ivy emerge from deep darkness, as if charged with electricity. Lombardi approaches image-making with scientific rigour and curiosity, capturing details with precision. Under her lens, every petal, vein and grain of pollen is rendered in astonishing clarity. 

@bibadesign_uvivf

Svetlana Talanova

Svetlana Talanova creates images by hand in the darkroom. PhotoSynthesis (2021) and No Less Than Others (2022) were both made directly on photosensitive paper by exposing natural materials to light. Talanova is interested in the shared patterns, that are repeated across the organic world, in both plants and humans. Veins are lit up with icy blues, teals, luminous yellows and greens, whilst some leaf edges appear torn, broken and fragmented. The aim of these pictures is, as Talanova explains, to illuminate “the delicate balance between growth and decline, erosion and deposition, light and dark, decay and rejuvenation.

svetlanatalanova.com | @svetlanatalanovastudio

Karine Laval

French-American photographer Karine Laval (b.1971) is intrigued by the idea of nature versus culture… familiar versus alien. In a cultivated garden, for example, species from across the world appear to live in unison. But most arrangements are, in truth, far from natural, unable to coexist without human intervention. She travels to private and public gardens across Europe and the USA to produce hallucinatory, fragmented images of flowers, leaves and grass. The results are disorientating and drenched in greens and pinks. Laval keeps experimentation alive in an era of digital manipulation. 

karinelavalstudio.com | @karinelaval
