After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation announced the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

“Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and Russia were back in the running for the Visitors’ Lions. As Antonia Majaca observed, the jury dared to apply a criterion, and the Biennale responded by dissolving judgment itself. 

Many artists have rejected this sham from the start. On the day the 2026 Biennale opened to the public, 54 artists in the international exhibition and 22 national pavilion teams withdrew from consideration in solidarity with the jury. In June, more than a hundred artists threatened legal action unless their names were removed from the ballot. Sunday’s ceremony awards a prize that few want to win.

The massive public pushback against the Biennale also demonstrates how close we have come to actualizing the moral principle that a genocidal, apartheid state has no legitimacy on any international stage. This year, we participated in a series of unprecedented protests. Biennale artists and cultural workers went on strike three times in seven months — nothing on this scale has ever happened before (not even during the anti-capitalist protests of 1968, which put a stop to the Biennale’s prizes for 18 years). This year’s protests were also unprecedented in terms of the level of collaboration between ANGA — which comprises artists, curators, and precariously employed workers — and rank-and-file labor unions. 

The Biennale is resolutely global, unfolding in the “anywhere or not at all” of the international art circuit. Against the false globalization of the art market, our internationalism was grounded in local organizing against Israel’s Zionist genocide.

The first of this year’s strikes, on May 8, was built locally in Venice, with Biennalocene, Sale Docks, and other local grassroots unions whose participation provided legal protection for striking art workers. On May 8, 30 of the Biennale’s 100 national pavilions closed partially or fully, and thousands of people marched from Via Garibaldi to the Arsenale, where they were met with police brutality. Many artists in the main exhibition draped or altered their works.

The second strike, on June 12, was national in scale. It was the result of a year of organizing assemblies and actions in about 20 cities all around Italy, with organizations including Mi Riconosci?, Vogliamo Tutt’Altro, Biennalocene, and grassroots unions through the Cultural Strike platform.

The third strike, on 30 October, responded to a call that emerged from outside the art world from the World Federation of Trade Unions and, in Italy, was taken up by militant dockworkers, including the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers, and the grassroots Unione Sindacale di Base. A network of port unions at 113 in 22 countries, including Italy, France, Greece, Turkey, and Morocco, refused to load weapons bound for Israel. This was the biggest ever coordinated action of its kind, and our role was to help build local participation in Venice.

Today, November 20, as this piece is being published, the International Student Strike brought further strike action to Venice, demonstrating the political convergence between students and the Biennale — students in the city are often employed in the cultural sector under precarious conditions.

Our ability to do this grew out of the work we began in 2024, in adherence to the guidelines of the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) and Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS), when our open letter demanding Israel’s exclusion from the Biennale was signed by more than 24,000 cultural workers. That year, the Israel pavilion closed. 

Between 2024 and 2026, our campaign connected more substantively with the Italian labor movement. As the June 12 strike articulated, the political atomization of artists is a labor issue, related to the art world’s reliance on precarity, which shifts the risk of political action onto individuals. The Biennale provides no fees or production money to artists, leaving them to fundraise their participation. Those whose work is not sufficiently market-friendly to claw back payment in future sales have to content themselves with being paid in the false currency of prestige.

ANGA refuses the oppressive logic that allows the Biennale to support genocide and profit from precarious labor while claiming to rise above politics. This year, we have made clear that the alliance we have created has the power to disrupt the Biennale’s functioning and change its nature. 

Today, the contradictions of the present political order — the indigestible, white-supremacy-coded cocktail of Europe’s simultaneous opposition to Russia and support for Israel; the flailing, ever-dying economy; the oceans of money poured into technologies of death and destruction — explode messily into the supposedly morally hermetic market-world of the Biennale.

The farcical “Visitors’ Lions” are the Biennale’s wager that the walls can always be painted pure white again. But this year’s massive actions have demonstrated that we will not allow Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine to be art-washed and ignored. ANGA’s members and supporters are no less steadfast than we were three years ago, when our campaign first began. It remains obvious and undeniable that Israel, the United States-backed abattoir-state, must not be allowed to bring its logic of butchery to be art-washed into neutral “complexity” at the Biennale. And we are now considerably more organized and better connected to the wider struggle against Zionism.  

When we look back to ANGA’s beginnings, in early 2024, we remember a time when the shock of total Zionist impunity was still raw enough to feel unreal. We could not imagine that friends or colleagues could disagree with this basic principle. We were soon disabused, as many cultural workers washed their hands of blood in service of their careers. 

But our collective efforts have transformed this anti-political status quo. The new compositions of struggle made possible by the mass revolt against Zionism offer a model for how the art world can reach beyond the isolated precarity of cultural labor into new alliances — with students, with dockworkers. The power of boycott as a tool has never been greater. We continue to remake the Venice Biennale, the modern world exhibition, from Walter Benjamin’s “place of pilgrimage to the commodity fetish” into a site of struggle.

item.title: So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges. 

For example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years. 

The following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing important work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab New Mexico.

Estate Planning

Ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist is alive, with someone available to guide the process and provide key information. Record contact information for key associates, including dealers and others, along with instructions for working with them. The estate will need access to digital assets, including archives, email correspondence, and computer files. Setting up a revocable trust can help the estate avoid probate, allowing assets and property to pass quickly to heirs, and also provides great privacy. 

When it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, said, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”

Inventories

One of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective, can strengthen future exhibition narratives. 

Stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt, which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.” 

When I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will. 

Appraisal

An appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish new cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.  

Choose appraisers carefully, and select those who are highly recommended. Deborah Gerstler Spanierman, a longtime art advisor and certified appraiser, recommends engaging “qualified and trustworthy allied professionals: appraisers, archivists, estate and foundation attorneys to handle the estate tax filing. Empower them to do their jobs and to work with the artist’s gallery, if they have one, which will all eventually support the artist’s legacy.”

Artist-Endowed Foundations

Artist-Endowed Foundations differ from other philanthropic measures because they create programs that feature the artist’s work. These may include organizing and lending to exhibitions, developing and publishing catalogue raisonnés, or operating education centers. 

Christine Vincent, the managing director of the Aspen Institute, an artist-endowed foundation initiative, explains: “Artists' estates and Artist-Endowed Foundations (AEFs) are entirely different things. Artists' estates are typically operated by private individuals and, as such, are not tax-exempt charitable entities. AEFs are tax-exempt charitable organizations with a mission to benefit the general public. An artist's estate may evolve into an AEF, for example under the estate plan of an artist's surviving spouse, but an AEF can never devolve into an artist's estate.”

Foundations also typically own the artist's intellectual property, including copyrights, trademarks, and in some cases, rights of personality. These are also used for public benefit, both to educate the public about the artist's oeuvre and to generate funds to support foundation programs. A governing board, often made up of art professionals and, in some cases, family members, typically guides the foundation’s activities. 

Storage and Conservation

Checking an artist’s archive for condition issues is essential. Identify which works need immediate care, which will need future restoration and/or repair, and act as promptly as possible. You might have to make difficult decisions about works that should be discarded or destroyed with the utmost consideration. Seek expert help — from conservators and other art professionals — when works require special treatment or present unique problems.

Where you store work also affects its condition. “Know how to properly store works on canvas and paper in temperature-controlled spaces, and insure them to avoid any future or potential loss,” says Jamieson Grillo, the sole trustee of the Estate of John Grillo. “If the estate can afford it, make sure you get your artwork conserved by a professional conservator with past experience and a proven track record in conserving similar art. Also, share any conservation reports with galleries you are working with.”

Galleries

Galleries with long-term relationships with artists will likely want to continue that partnership after an artist passes away. But estates seeking new representation should start by identifying suitable galleries, looking at those that handle works similar to the estate’s. 

Prioritize and prepare before contacting any galleries. Gallery owner Hollis Taggart swears by making it as easy as possible for the gallery by providing as much detail as possible. “The more organized an estate is, the more likely a gallery will be to take on the heavy lifting of representing that estate.” Taggart also advises a clear vision: “Be as supportive as possible by organizing an inventory list of the works so the gallery knows right up front what the estate holdings are, and how big a project is involved.” 

Museums

Placing works in museum collections helps enhance and maintain an artist’s reputation and legacy. But museums often hesitate to accept donations because of limited exhibition and storage space. Patti Smith, an art collections manager at the Stephenson Ceramics Studio, suggests approaching them thoughtfully and presenting only high-quality works, or collaborating with a gallery to develop a “gifting exhibition.” She says, “I helped develop one for the estate of artist Richard Wilt (1915–1981) that documented a body of his work and displayed it in the gallery. We approached new museums as well as museums that already had his work. Since there was demand for purchasing the work, once the museums made their selections, the work was offered up for sale, and 100% of the proceeds went to the Richard Wilt Foundation at the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design.”

Web Presence

Estates should have websites that include an artist biography, a timeline, a gallery of works, and contact information. This can help anyone doing research — including appraisers and dealers — and may also help locate lost works. 

A social media presence, especially regular Instagram posts, keeps an artist’s legacy in the public consciousness. Mary Clare McKinley of the Richard Diebenkorn Foundation says, “When estates and foundations harness the power of social media, it can be a brilliant tool for education, legacy and community building. In my opinion, investing in research is always a good decision. Then, consider the platform a way to share information less formally than publishing a book, and creatively explore ways to use it: Enjoy the flexibility, interactivity, and immediate access to a wider public.” She shares that the Diebenkorn Foundation’s Instagram posts “highlight scholars making exciting discoveries, support museum exhibitions, feature [their] own intriguing archival finds, and suggest new visual connections to Diebenkorn’s work.”

Image Rights

According to the Center for Art Law, when an artist passes, their estate has two seemingly conflicting tasks: "to protect an artist’s work by exercising exclusive rights over them, and to disseminate their artwork to the public to establish a lasting legacy and placement in the art world.” But this dilemma runs parallel to another issue: Should estates prioritize revenue, or improve public access to art?  

One recurring issue involves image use and rights, and estates typically turn to licensing agencies for support. For example, Artist’s Rights Society guides clients through obtaining copyright and intellectual property clearance, legal support, and advocacy. Recently, as estates have tried to balance revenue and reputation, and deal with the easy proliferation of web-based images, some have become less concerned with enforcing image rights. 

Auctions

Auction results, now widely available through online databases, are key public indicators of an artist’s salability. Selling an especially strong work at auction is a gamble some estates take to establish a benchmark for an artist whose work lacks a previous auction record. Estates of recognized artists may want to partner with an auction house to mount a significant sale. 

To do so, an estate needs to meet certain standards. Wendy Battleson, senior vice president at Bonhams, says, “Auction houses, in general, are looking for an estate with an established record of sales at relatively high values (five to six figures minimum), ideally sold publicly. We also look at the amount of inventory available in order to continue to tell the artist’s story over a period of time. The beauty of working with an auction house is that pricing is public, and there is rarely a concern that the art has been sold for less than market rate. With a dealer, the sales are typically private, so you don’t know if you could have achieved a higher price.”

item.title: El Greco Masterpiece Gets Its Colors Back After More Than 400 Years - ARTnews.com
item.description:
King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco’s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it. The following four centuries of dirt, varnish, and enthusiastic repainting hadn’t done the picture any favors, either.

A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned. The muddy browns and sickly greens that had dulled the picture for generations are gone. In their place are brilliant blues, reds, yellows, and purples, along with a newfound depth that had been buried beneath grime.

The restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings. The project was supported by the Fundacion Callia in partnership with Spain’s Patrimonio Nacional, which oversees the country’s royal collections.

The results were reported in detail by El País, whose writer followed the restoration from the painting’s removal from El Escorial in February through its finished restoration in October. And what a job it was.

Alonso had initially expected the restoration to take about four months. But once he and fellow restorer Adela Murgui began cleaning the enormous canvas, which measures nearly 15 feet high and 10 feet wide, they discovered that its condition was far worse than even feared.

“When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Centuries of varnish and repainting had darkened the colors and flattened the composition. In the 19th century, he explained, painters had simply painted over damaged areas, often adding their own interpretations of what El Greco intended.

The restorers spent months carefully stripping away those additions, revealing the original paint beneath. Afterward, the repaired the damaged areas using soluble materials, taking pains not to add anything that couldn’t be removed later.

The restoration is particularly striking given the painting’s rather unhappy beginnings.

El Greco painted The Martyrdom between 1580 and 1582 for the basilica at El Escorial, Philip II’s vast monastery and palace outside Madrid. The king wanted a powerful statement of Catholic faith, while the artist hoped the commission might secure him a permanent position as a court painter.

Neither’s wish was totally granted.

Rather than concentrate on the grisly execution of Saint Maurice and his fellow Christian soldiers, El Greco pushed the violence into the background. Up front, he placed a group of handsome soldiers in brightly colored clothing, their elongated bodies and theatrical poses exemplary of the skills he had learned in Venice and Rome.

Philip II apparently admired the painting’s quality, paying the artist a substantial sum of 800 ducats, but felt it wasn’t right for its intended religious setting. The work was relegated to another room, and El Greco never clinched the royal appointment he’d hoped for.

The painting stayed there for most of the next 444 years, apart from a trip to Madrid for an exhibition in 1999, all the while gradually losing most of its remarkable color and atmosphere.

The restoration also marks another achievement for the Fundacion Callia, founded by Carmen Reviriego, which has helped restore works by Zurbarán, Rubens, Brueghel the Elder, Velázquez, and others through its partnership with Madrid’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando. According to El País, the foundation has helped mobilize €5 million for the preservation of artworks.

When ARTnews spoke with Reviriego in March, she described Callia as an “incubator of patrons,” bringing together collectors and philanthropists from Spain, Latin America, and beyond. Her goal is to encourage a stronger culture of private support for the arts in a country that has traditionally relied heavily on public funding.

Reviriego had specifically mentioned The Martyrdom during that interview as an example of the work the foundation hoped to support. “El Greco was the Jeff Koons or Damien Hirst of his day,” she told ARTnews this week, “and Phillip II was the most power man and greatest patron of the 16th century.”

There’s a nice historical symmetry here. Reviriego argued that great works of art are rarely the achievement of an artist alone. Without patrons, many wouldn’t exist at all. She pointed to the Royal Collections themselves, built in part through the patronage of Philip II, the very king who commissioned The Martyrdom more than four centuries ago. Now, private patronage has helped give that painting a new life.

For Alonso, meanwhile, the completed restoration marks something of a farewell. After decades spent working on El Greco’s paintings, he told El País that The Martyrdom was the last of the artist’s great masterpieces still awaiting restoration.

The newly restored painting is expected to go on temporary display at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery before returning to El Escorial. This time, visitors will get a much better idea of what Philip II saw more than four centuries ago.

item.title: Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History - Hyperallergic
item.description:
AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama. 

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition. 

“A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.” 

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process. 

The first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning. 

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”

By early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she says. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.” 

Within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

The exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”

item.title: Grand Theft Auto VI ’s Vice City Pays Homage to the Bass, Among More Art Easter Eggs - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The new Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.

Rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling.

Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. Months ago, a screenshot circulated online from an expansion for Grand Theft Auto Online, showing a new character in a shirt with an “Art Oregano” logo. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”

Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a new version of Art Oregano may appear.

I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night mundanely, mostly comparing paint swatches. All of it in line with what viral clips suggest: the game’s characters can do drugs and rob banks—chaos, generally speaking—but we’d rather have time to drive with no destination in mind.

Before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our plans to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

item.title: Judge Allows Lawsuit Over Allegedly Stolen Fra Angelico to Move Forward - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A New York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.

In a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, New York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.

“No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen.

As ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.

According to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family says Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.

Feigen, one of New York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.

The Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.

Feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have said they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.

Which brings us to the latest ruling.

Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.

But stolen art can be a tricky business under New York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.

Things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes said there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the issue now.

The judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.

Feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

item.title: How do Artworks Acquire Value? New York Art Dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky Weigh In. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
How do artworks acquire value? I discussed this complex question with two New York art dealers during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.

David Nolan, whose eponymous gallery has been open since 1987, gave the view of an art world veteran; Anton Svyatsky, who opened Management in 2023, provided a newer perspective.

Along the way, we discussed the role of the collector in sustaining value, the challenges of pricing artworks by emerging artists, the ways in which influence and market value have become decoupled, the casino that is the auction house and the zoo that is the art fair.

At our talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Svyatsky insisted that collectors need to see themselves as responsible for an artist’s value, rather than depend on dealers and institutions for that function. This shift in perspective, and a return to collecting artists in depth, may well be the key to ridding the art world of speculators. Nolan recalled the immense changes that took place during the 1980s, and the increasing attention paid to artworks’ financial value.

Speaking of casinos, a flask emerged at the mention of the new partnership between Artnet and Kalshi—you can catch that moment and other choice ones in the video of the talk above.

item.title: Working Mothers Face Pervasive Discrimination in London Art World, Study Finds - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a new study. As reported by the Art Newspaper today, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.

The study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, looked at the extent to which pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused on lower-paid, non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing.

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent said they had been explicitly denied promotion.

The authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent said their workplace had a specific parental leave policy. They additionally blamed the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.

Class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study suggests. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination daunting, with many women instead choosing to take a less senior position, move into freelance work, or leave the art world.

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”

item.title: A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

Rei Xiao, Brooklyn, New York

How long have you been working in this space?

Two years.

Describe an average day in your studio.

I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin.

I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

item.title: Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam’s Embroideries in Green - Colossal
item.description:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness. Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.

The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram.

item.title: Dramatic Waves Crash on Iceland’s Coast in Photos by Vilhelm Gunnarsson - Colossal
item.description:
Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.

Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

item.title: Was Grandma Moses a Foil to Modernity, or a Product of It? - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Grandma Moses’s landmark survey at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Arkansas opens with a flash of fire. A scene of a bridge burning in Troy is ablaze in red and orange; another painting, Fire in the Woods (1940), crackles with flames and smoke. This emphasis on fire, thunderstorms, and extreme weather in the first room seems to be an anticipatory rebuke to any potential complaints about Moses’s relentless good cheer. Despite a long and often sorrow-filled life—Anna Mary Robertson (“Grandma”) Moses lost five of her 10 children in infancy—Moses held fast to life’s joys in her art, and most of the paintings in the show are happy scenes of work, celebration, and family.

Starting with fire does prime the viewer to recognize the heat of Moses’s oeuvre, an intensity she channeled into careful, repetitive marks—tidy stacks of hay, carefully shaded leaves, the checkered grid of farm fields. Cambridge Valley (1942) is a scene of steady eye, mind, and hand, an expansive view of the New York countryside rendered with lovingly topographic attention. There’s almost no loss of detail as you look across the valley, a result of Moses’s unhurried care. People appear in nearly all her works, simply rendered and adding elements of humor, like a man’s hat blown off by the wind in 1948’s The Thunderstorm, a perfect “O” flush against the picture plane. The fire returns, however, in Moses’s many maple sugaring scenes, flames licking the base of large pots in which sap is boiled down. Even snow scenes are made to sparkle, radiating light through Moses’s use of glitter, a new technology she applied amply to her canvases against the advice of her dealer.

Moses was no stranger to patient work, having spent her life on farms in New York state and Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. Her memory of these years provided ample subject matter for the painting she took up in her late 70s, though one of the claims of the exhibition was that Moses was making art her whole life. A fireboard from 1918 was what she called her first “large picture,” while yarn pictures from the 1930s show her capacity to work with a limited palette of solid colors. These craft activities, usually cordoned off from the realm of serious art, gave Moses a point of entry into visual representation as a way of telling her own story.

Spanning 101 years, from 1860 to 1961, her life story ran parallel with a century of massive transformation and the rapid emergence of a modern, industrial world. That her style and subject matter remain largely unchanged over the course of her decades-long painting career—the 80 some works in the show have more similarities than differences—suggests Moses’s indifference to the revolutions happening around her. Instead, the exhibition catalog argues, Moses was in dialog with changing notions of the elderly, the increasing representation of labor in 20th-century art, and Cold War politics that sought to export a vision of American goodness.

Was Grandma Moses a foil to modernity, or a product of it? While her work eschews direct portrayals of industry, she reportedly solved the compositional dilemma of capturing sprawling valleys by glimpsing a reflection in a hubcap, introducing the gleam of the automobile into what feel like entirely timeless views. Her art was held up by contemporaries as an example of the “primitive,” exhibited as the quaint musings of an aging farmwife. She seemed to give America a soul, something it appeared to be lacking in the postwar era of big capital. And yet she amassed quite a lot of capital herself, through lucrative partnerships with Hallmark among other companies. She was media-savvy, appearing on talk shows and in documentaries, leveraging the perceived powerlessness of a little old woman to charm and disarm her critics. In the end, there’s nothing more modern than nostalgia for the lost authenticity of the countryside, an authenticity Moses returns us to in her sincerely merry paintings.

item.title: Memphis Art Museum: Reconsidering the Stories Art Tells - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
What does a museum make visible, and what remains outside its frame? That question runs through the inaugural programme of Memphis Art Museum, which opens its new Herzog & de Meuron-designed campus on 6 December 2026. Instead of presenting its collection as a settled account of artistic achievement, the museum brings works from different periods and traditions into contact, drawing attention to the ways art is made, interpreted and valued. At the centre of the programme is Making Beauty: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907–1984, which places the work of a Black photographic studio at the heart of this reconsideration. Around it, new commissions and thematic presentations explore the relationship between artistic form, lived experience and the institutions that shape cultural memory.

Memphis’s new museum also arrives at a moment when galleries are rethinking how people use and experience public cultural spaces. Recent openings and expansions – including BRUSK in Bruges, the International Centre for the Image in Dublin, V&A East Museum in London, the expanded New Museum in New York and LACMA’s David Geffen Galleries in Los Angeles – suggest that the gallery is increasingly expected to be more than a place to view exhibitions. Audiences may come for a particular artist, but they also arrive to meet, learn, attend performances, spend time in shared spaces or simply find somewhere to be. Free access, extended hours, public plazas and programmes that connect art with music and everyday life acknowledge that cultural participation is not always planned around a visit to a single exhibition. The response to these new spaces – from the crowds at BRUSK’s pre-opening weekend to the tens of thousands who attended LACMA’s opening celebrations – points to a continuing appetite for collective cultural experiences. It also raises a practical civic question: as cities change, are there enough welcoming places where people can encounter art without specialist knowledge or a particular income?

Memphis itself is more than the setting for the museum’s programme. Its river, musical traditions, architecture and communities inform how individual works are encountered. The four new commissions make this connection particularly tangible, although each approaches place through a distinct visual language. Jordan Ann Craig’s Sharp Tongue; The Sky and the Heart Aflame (2026), installed in the rooftop art garden, translates patterns drawn from Northern Cheyenne and other Plains Native American beadwork into monumental abstraction. As light shifts and visitors move around it, the work changes in appearance, bringing Indigenous artistic knowledge into dialogue with the Mississippi River landscape.

Yunhee Min’s Impressions (bluffs, mounds, landing) begins with a different reading of the terrain. Developed from rubbings made at sites around Memphis, the installation combines a 92-yard woven curtain with a 66-foot lenticular work across the museum’s street-facing windows. Sloping forms recall Mississippian mounds, while the curtain evokes the movement of water. Min turns the building’s surfaces into part of the composition, so that the work shifts between image, architecture and environment. Where Craig draws on the visual language of beadwork, Min builds an impression of the city from traces of its landscape.

Carlos Rosales-Silva’s Alma del rio (2026), painted across three walls of the parking structure, offers a more direct urban portrait. Sassafras leaves, the roofline of Rust Hall, ceremonial mounds and Isaac Hayes’s desk at Stax Records appear among its motifs. Natural history, architecture and musical culture share the same visual field, resisting any single definition of Memphis identity. On the rooftop, Eso Tolson’s A Memphis for You(2026) uses hand lettering and typography to address residents and visitors through a phrase encountered in fragments. Both works make the city legible through details that might otherwise be passed over, turning public space into a place of recognition and discovery.

The rooftop brings these commissions into conversation with two sculptures that unsettle ideas of landscape and commemoration. Sean Scully’s Stack Blues (2017) uses stacked shades of blue to evoke the meeting of sky and water, acquiring particular resonance in a city associated with the blues. The Smoke Coin (2025), a collaborative bronze by LaKela Brown and Mario Moore, asks who is considered worthy of appearing on currency. One face carries Moore’s portrait of Brown; the other bears a relief of collard greens. Positioned above the Mississippi, across from the Cotton Exchange, the sculpture places the language of monetary value against a landscape shaped by the movement of enslaved people. Its location makes the histories behind wealth and the symbols through which societies honour it difficult to separate.

Recognition is also at the centre of Making Beauty, curated by C. Rose Smith and organised with the National Civil Rights Museum. Drawing on an archive of more than 100,000 photographs, the exhibition presents 163 images by the Hooks Brothers, whose Memphis studio documented Black life across much of the twentieth century. Five thematic strands move between portraiture, fashion, music, photographic practice and political uplift. The title describes the studio’s philosophy of making beauty not as an ornamental ideal, but as an assertion of self-definition during the Jim Crow era and beyond. Through pose, dress, lighting and setting, these photographs show people shaping how they wished to be seen.

That distinction is important. Photography is often discussed as a means of documenting social reality, while the artistic decisions involved in making an image receive less attention, particularly when the photographers and subjects have been marginalised by established accounts of the medium. The exhibition’s selection of studio portraits, documentary photographs, advertising work and negatives brings the Hooks Brothers’ technical skill and visual judgement into focus. Placing their practice alongside photographers including James Van Der Zee, Addison Scurlock, Seydou Keita and James Barnor also connects the Memphis studio to a wider history of photography across the African diaspora. As Chief Curator Dr Patricia Lee Daigle argues, the brothers deserve recognition not only as chroniclers of their community, but as artists whose work belongs within the history of photography. A related exhibition at the National Civil Rights Museum and the 2027 Black Portraiture[s] conference extend this enquiry.

The collection presentations broaden the programme, with their strongest contributions emerging through the encounters they create between works. The River Calling: Storytelling in Memphis and the Mississippi Deltaconsiders how folklore, music and regional experience inform visual narratives, bringing works by William Eggleston, Frederick J. Brown, Carroll Cloar, Ahmad George and Carl E. Moore into a shared frame. Its focus on storytelling offers an entry into the museum’s regional holdings without suggesting that Southern identity can be contained in a single image. In Towards Liberation, a stained-glass window made by Henry Sharp Studio in 1877 is placed alongside works by Martha Rosler, Jacob Lawrence, Romare Bearden and Elizabeth Catlett. The window’s depiction of a Black Jesus – possibly the first public example of its kind in the United States – gives the presentation a striking focal point.

Other displays examine the assumptions built into familiar categories of art history. Speaking in Shapes looks beyond the conventional association of geometric abstraction with European modernism, bringing together artists including Samuel Levi-Jones, Elizabeth Murray, Dyani White Hawk and Memphis-born James Little. Its attention to women artists and artists of colour exposes an imbalance in the reception of abstraction: some makers have been expected to explain their work through identity, while others have been free to occupy the supposedly universal territory of formal experimentation. White Hawk’s Round Dance (2023), which brings Lakota aesthetic traditions into contact with modern abstraction, makes that division especially difficult to sustain. Here, cultural specificity and formal innovation are not competing claims; they are part of the same artistic language.

The presentation of women in European art between 1500 and 1680 receives attention in Power and Absence: Women in Europe, 1500–1680. Its examination of how women were depicted in Renaissance and Early Baroque art sits alongside the work of Sofonisba Anguissola, one of the few women artists recognised among the period’s masters. Her Portrait of One of the Artist’s Sisters and Self-Portrait, both dated 1560, offer a counterpoint to images of women produced largely by male artists. Elsewhere, Medieval Bodies considers how religious art made between approximately 1000 and 1550 used the human figure to communicate social roles, national boundaries, racial identities and beliefs about the afterlife. Together, these presentations encourage viewers to look again at images that might otherwise appear familiar, attending to the values and conventions embedded in their making.

The programme also accommodates artistic languages that resist straightforward classification. Rhapsodies in Black traces the influence of jazz on Black American abstraction, connecting Sam Gilliam’s gestural compositions with later work by Torkwase Dyson and James Little. Its accompanying soundtrack makes rhythm and improvisation audible as well as visible. In Head to the Sky, more than 100 works consider the breadth of Black American life, from political struggle to leisure, intimacy and sport. Works by Jordan Casteel, Titus Kaphar, Ernest C. Withers and Derek Fordjour refuse to confine Black experience to a single narrative of adversity. Meanwhile, An Inner Vision follows the development of American abstraction through works by Georgia O’Keeffe, Willem de Kooning, Cecily Brown and Pacita Abad, while Things to Come turns to artists’ changing visions of technology and the future.

Across the programme, the museum’s architecture becomes more than a container for its collection. The rooftop garden, street-facing windows and public-facing commissions allow Memphis to enter the building in different ways – through its landscape, its visual traditions and the details of everyday life. That relationship is significant in a city whose cultural identity is widely celebrated, yet whose histories of labour, racial exclusion and economic exchange remain inseparable from its present. By placing the Hooks Brothers’ portraits alongside contemporary responses to abstraction, public memory and the Mississippi, the museum creates room for these strands to be seen together without smoothing over their differences. The result is not a definitive portrait of Memphis, but an invitation to look at the city from several positions at once. As visitors move between the galleries and the works beyond them, the collection’s story becomes something encountered, tested and revised – with Memphis itself always in the frame.

Memphis Art Museum opens 6 December: memphisartmuseum.org

Words: Shirley Stevenson
