item.title: Christie’s Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt - ARTnews.com
item.description:
At its packed Rockefeller Center saleroom on Tuesday night, Christie’s staged a sometimes lively, sometimes listless two-hour-and-40-minute sale of 20th-century art, led by an $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The house estimated the 74-lot sale to bring $511–$743 million, once adjusted for five works withdrawn before the sale. (Along the withdrawn works was a Frida Kahlo estimated at $2 to $3.5 million, which was pulled just hours before the proceedings were set to begin.) The hammer total for the night came to $521.1 million, slightly above the low estimate. With the house’s fees added, the sale totaled $626.6 million.

Records were set for Hans Bellmer, Fernando Botero, Wassily Kandinsky, Wifredo Lam, and Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem. At the same time, there were some failures to launch: works by Fernand Léger, Henri Matisse, Joan Mitchell, Amedeo Modigliani, Henry Moore, and Jackson Pollock did not sell. Still, the house found buyers for 68 of the 74 lots offered, for a healthy sell-through rate of 92 percent.

In the room were market players who formed a walking power list. Among them were dealers Jeffrey Deitch, Larry Gagosian, Thaddaeus Ropac, Christophe van de Weghe, and Dominique Lévy and Brett Gorvy, as well as advisors including Amy Cappellazzo, Kim Heirston, Laura Paulson, and Jussi Pylkkänen, formerly the house’s global president. Royalty for the night was David Nahmad, whose family offered the Kandinsky. He sat in his customary spot in the front row and was the underbidder on a few lots, including the Picasso painting Le Baiser, consigned by artist Jeff Koons.

Christie’s equivalent sale last year, which combined selections from the collection of Robert and Patricia Ross Weis with the 20th-century evening sale, totaled a whopping $690 million, making Tuesday’s take 9 percent lower.

Tuesday night’s sale started slow, with the first four lots hammering below estimate, though the last of those, Hans Bellmer’s Jointure de boules (La Poupée), set a new auction record for the artist at $1.67 million with fees. The bidding picked up after that, with a strong showing of in-the-room bidders peppered among the specialists on the phone and a very active online bidder from Florida. Works by Yves Tanguy and Isamu Noguchi hammered well above estimate after spirited bidding, at $4.6 million and $1.2 million, respectively. The Noguchi hammered for double its high estimate; with fees, the price landed at $1.54 million.

That energy carried the crowd well into the star lot of the evening, Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1922–23), which bore a $60–$80 million estimate. Before the sale, the house said the work was guaranteed to set a new record. It sold after a short bidding war between Christie’s global president Alex Rotter; Sara Friedlander, chairman of postwar and contemporary art, Americas; and art advisor Ralph DeLuca. Rotter came away the victor, with the winning $74 million bid. With fees, the work landed at $85.8 million, nearly doubling Kandinsky’s previous high of $44.8 million, paid for the artist’s 1910 painting Murnau mit Kirche II (Murnau with Church II) at Sotheby’s London in 2023.

Partway through the sale, DeLuca said of the results, in a text to ARTnews, “The flight to quality is astounding.” That description was as apt for Tuesday’s bidders as it was for DeLuca. He was the underbidder on a number of top lots Tuesday night and lost the Kandinsky by only one bid. (Per the Baer Faxt, De Luca was the winner of the Tanguy.)

To wit, the Claude Monet picture Champ d’avoine et coquelicots, offered three lots later, drew bids from three phone bidders as well as two bidders in the room. That activity sent the painting, which comes from the collection of William I. Koch, soaring past its $12–$18 million estimate. It hammered for $22 million, or $26 million with fees. The Auguste Rodin sculpture Le Penseur, taille de la porte dit “moyen modèle,” offered next and also from the Koch collection, hammered at $6.4 million. With fees, it came to $7.9 million, more than double the high estimate. Another Monet offered later in the sale, La berge du Petit-Gennevilliers, drew the longest bidding of the evening (nine minutes), though one could blame auctioneer Adrien Meyer for some leniency there. Ada Tsui, senior vice president and head of 20th/21st century art for Asia Pacific, and Arco Yu, an associate vice president and specialist who heads the 20th and 21st century art evening sale for Asia Pacific, traded bids in interminable $100,000 increments while they stood shoulder to shoulder, to take the work from a $5 million starting bid to its eventual hammer price of $10.5 million, just a smidge above the $10 million high estimate. With fees, the work’s total came to $12.8 million.

The biggest fireworks came a handful of lots later, when Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915–16) hammered for $71 million after a five-minute contest between Max Carter, the house’s global chairman, and Rotter, who again came away with the prize. The hammer price came smack in the middle of the $60–$80 million estimate, but with fees, it landed at $82.3 million.

By contrast, seven works consigned by Jeff Koons failed to ignite much excitement. The combined low estimate for the group was $104 million, but the hammer total fell shy, at just $87.8 million, with four pieces coming in below their low estimates. With fees, the group totaled, coincidentally, $104 million. The set was led by the Picasso Le Baiser, which hammered at $26.5 million, far below its $40 million low estimate; with fees, the piece brought $31.2 million. A bright spot came with a large canvas by Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem, Hercules and Achelous. Though it hammered for $11.5 million, shy of its $12 million low estimate, it sold for $13.9 million with the house’s fees, setting a new record for the Dutch Old Master. Other works by Picasso, Tilman Riemenschneider, and Édouard Manet filled out the group; see a full report here.

The energy seemed to peter out considerably after the sale of La berge du Petit-Gennevilliers, which followed the Koons trove. Five of the six unsold lots came in the back half of the sale, and 14 of the following 46 lots hammered below estimate. Of the 11 lots in that grouping that overperformed, Diego Rivera’s Vendedora de flores, de Tehuantepec, from the Koch collection, proved the biggest surprise, as four specialists duked it out over seven minutes of bidding before the work hammered for $8.1 million, more than double the $3.5 million high estimate. Sophie Jensen, a client advisory associate, won the contest. The total with fees came to $10 million, within spitting distance of Rivera’s auction record of $14.1 million, set at Christie’s New York in 2022.

Rounding out the night’s top 10 were works by Alberto Giacometti, Henri Matisse, and Mark Rothko. (Noticing a theme here?) The Giacometti, a four-foot-high 1949 bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no. 2), a trademark elongated rendition of a woman, was offered without reserve and with an estimate of $20–$30 million. The collector Herbert Lust had bought it from Chicago collector Joseph R. Shapiro in 1970, and it had been off the market ever since. It hammered for $22 million to a phone bidder via Katharine Arnold, the house’s vice chairman and head of postwar and contemporary art, after a three-minute contest. With fees, the result was $26 million, good for the fifth-best result of the evening.

While it hammered below its $10–$15 million estimate, Wifredo Lam’s Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) did break a record for the artist. After a handful of bids, it hammered for $9.5 million, or $11.6 million with fees. His previous auction record was $9.6 million, set at Sotheby’s New York in 2020. (The winner, again per Baer Faxt, was collector Gary Nader, also the reported winner of Jean-Michel Basquiat’s Untitled (Fist), which sold for $6.2 million with fees.)

Similarly, Fernando Botero’s Horse, the 11-foot-tall rotund bronze sculpture currently residing outside Rockefeller Center, landed within estimate but broke a record for the artist. The work hammered for $4.2 million to a bidder on the phone with Maria Los, deputy chairman and head of client advisory for the Americas. The total with fees of $5.24 million squeaked it past his previous top result of $5.1 million, set at Christie’s in 2023 for the 1979 painting The Musicians.

Tuesday night’s sale was the second of the week, following Sotheby’s two-part Monday night sale, which generated $378.7 million across 74 lots. A sale of works from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum netted $110 million, followed by the house’s Now and Contemporary Art sale, which fetched $268.8 million. Other major sales will follow at Sotheby’s and Christie’s on Wednesday and Thursday nights, respectively.

New York gallerist and art advisor Cristin Tierney put the sale in the context of tech failures at banks, the national air travel system, and even the National Security Agency that plagued the U.S. in the run-up to the sale. “Days and days of software outages, air travel chaos and stock volatility,” she told ARTnews in a text partway through the sale, “but you know what you can count on? Art. Turns out a market based on supporting culture, belief and creativity is the most consistent one of all.”

Advisor Gabriela Palmieri reached for an aviation metaphor to describe the evening. “This week is a congested airspace,” she said in a conversation outside the saleroom. “The houses are doing the most amazing job, because they have to land a lot of planes. There’s incredible elasticity in the market, but the sheer volume of lots is staggering. Anything that fell short, you know, the market is recalibrating. Buyers are drawing the line in certain places. But the houses are achieving a lot of beautiful results.”

item.title: Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons’s Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie’s, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Jeff Koons has long been an art collector. As far back as 2010, when the New York Times visited “one of the world’s most famous living artists,” his Upper East Side home held works by artists ranging from the French Realist Gustave Courbet and the Rococo painter Jean-Honoré Fragonard to the Impressionist Édouard Manet and the 16th-century Antwerp painter Quentin Massys. He had generally avoided discussing his collection, the Times wrote, “out of discretion and privacy.”

Collectors and the public are getting another look at that collection this week. Nine works consigned to Christie’s New York came from the artist’s holdings, according to two unnamed industry sources who spoke to the Times this fall. The sources said the house had guaranteed Koons a minimum price and that he planned to plow the proceeds toward his famously expensive art production. (Christie’s has identified the seller only as “a distinguished collector.”)

Seven of the works, grouped under the title “Heroes and Lovers,” were offered at the house’s 20th-century art sale on Tuesday. Together they were estimated at $104 million to $153.5 million. The low end alone is slightly more than the $91.1 million Christie’s got in 2019 for Koons’s own 1986 sculpture Rabbit. The other two works will be offered during the house’s Classic Week next year.

The group did not perform particularly well in the end, hammering for a total of just $87.8 million in total, well shy of the low estimate; with the house’s fees, the group sold for $104 million. No lot exceeded its estimate; four fell short of their low estimates. Four of the works sold at an inflation-adjusted loss.

Leading the pack with four works, including the top-estimated piece, was Pablo Picasso; the sale also included examples by Fragonard, Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem, François Le Moyne, Édouard Manet, and Tilman Riemenschneider.

Accounting for up to 60 percent of the total estimate for the sale was Picasso’s Le Baiser (1969), showing two lovers entwined in a kiss and estimated at $40 million–$60 million. Koons bought it at Sotheby’s in 2008 for $17.4 million ($27.1 million, adjusted for inflation). It has hung on the walls of institutions from the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris to London’s National Gallery and New York’s Guggenheim Museum. But the splashy provenance and exhibition history couldn’t get it to its low estimate. It hammered for just $26.5 million to a man bidding in the room, to sell for $31.2 million with the house’s fees.

Picasso’s 1941 canvas Tête de femme (Dora Maar), showing the photographer who was then his lover, was estimated at $25 million–$35 million. Koons acquired it in 2007 at Christie’s New York for $16.3 million ($26.1 million, adjusted for inflation). It barely squeaked by its low estimate to hammer at $25.5 million to the house’s Katharine Arnold, vice-chairman and head of post-war and contemporary art, selling for $30 million million with fees.

He purchased the Spaniard’s Couple (1969), showing a duo in an embrace, at Sotheby’s London in 2011, paying $10.5 million ($15.8 million, adjusted for inflation); it was estimated at $12 million–$18 million. It had not been exhibited since a 1970 show at the Palais des Papes in Avignon, France. It hammered for $13 million to Christie’s global president Alex Rotter, or $15.6 million with fees.

The Spanish artist’s Tête de femme (1939–40) was estimated at $10 million–$15 million. The piece had passed through the hands of the legendary American collectors Burton and Emily Tremaine in the 1940s and the dealer Larry Gagosian in the ’80s. Koons acquired it at Sotheby’s Paris in 2012 for $7.9 million ($11.5 million, adjusted for inflation). It hammered to deputy chairman Olivier Camu for just $6 million, to sell for $7.4 million with fees.

Bound to set a record was the Dutch painter Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem’s 8-foot-wide canvas Hercules and Achelous (1590), which was estimated at $12 million–$18 million. The artist’s previous high was $8.1 million, achieved by the same painting at the same auction house in 2008, when Tuesday’s seller acquired it. It was on loan to New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art from then until 2018. That $8.1 million far exceeds the artist’s second-highest price, $1.7 million, set with The Raising of Lazarus (1602) at Christie’s London in 2023. It hammered to Andrew Fletcher, global head of the old masters department, for $11.5 million, just shy of its low estimate, to sell for $13.9 million with fees.

A wooden sculpture by the German artist Tilman Riemenschneider, Saint Catherine (ca. 1505), bore a $4 million–$6 million estimate. Koons bought it at Sotheby’s New York in 2008 for $6.3 million ($10 million, adjusted for inflation), setting the artist’s still-standing record, and then lent it to the Met, where it remained on view until 2019. (That price is double his second-highest, which is, in turn, nearly six times his third-highest.) It hammered within estimate for $4.5 million to François de Poortere, head of old masters for New York, or $5.6 million with fees, shy of what Tuesday night’s seller paid for it.

The cheapest piece on offer from the Koons trove was a Manet pastel, Femme au tub (ca. 1878–79), estimated at $1 million–$1.5 million. Koons paid $2.3 million for it at Sotheby’s London in 2014 ($3.3 million, adjusted for inflation). He lent it to a show that appeared at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Getty and to another at the Met. It hammered shy of the low estimate at $800,000, or $1 million with fees, less than half what the seller paid for it.

item.title: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for.

When the “Monument Against Fascism” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque.

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.

item.title: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Smoke presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires.

The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty.

item.title: Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Olivia Reavey moves at breakneck speed. Her silver-gelatin-analog printing process is frenzied and intense: Black-and-white prints are cut into irregular quadrilaterals with crumpled edges, then hung unframed and loosely fixed to the walls with clips, pins, and other supports. But this is not just slapdash; everything here is intentionally energetic and playful, with images asserting the body’s formal pleasure captured in film.

Many bare their flesh but are often obfuscated or appear with objects: a broken branch covers a male’s buttocks in “Stick” (all works 2026); a wooden lever protrudes from a woman’s pubic area, captured in the reflection of a mirror in “Untitled.” The penetrative and phallic elements here are obvious, but also read neutrally in a recurring tension between eroticism and form — shapes and tonal values outweigh anything provocative.

item.title: Amid Legal Controversy, Christie’s Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Christie’s pulled a Frida Kahlo painting from an evening sale hours before it was to be auctioned amid a debate over whether the work was legally permitted to leave Mexico.

“In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research. We look forward to selling this work at a later date,” a spokesperson for Christie’s told ARTnews. The work, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $2 million to $3.5 million, was to be included in the 20th Century Evening Sale in New York, scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. on November 17.

In the days leading up to the sale, Mexico’s cultural authorities had faced accusations of failing to protect the painting, which is considered part of the nation’s heritage and legally protected. An online campaign argued that the 1952 work, titled Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (Congress of the Peoples for Peace), was part of the trust that Kahlo’s husband, the artist Diego Rivera, created for the Casa Azul after her death in 1954 and that it cannot legally leave the country. It is unclear where the painting was held prior to it coming to New York for this week’s auction.

The Frida Kahlo Museum told ARTnews that the painting is part of an ongoing investigation by Mexican authorities. At the time of publication, the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL), which is responsible for the country’s patrimony, maintained that Kahlo donated it during her lifetime and that it left Mexico before her work was declared an artistic monument in 1984.

In a statement Monday, the collective behind the campaign, Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection), called on INBAL to stop the sale of Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. The collective asserts that the oil-on-masonite work was among the hundreds of artworks and objects at Casa Azul that Rivera inventoried after Kahlo’s death, when he established the trust. The inventory, the collective says, carried explicit instructions from Rivera that the items remain on the premises both during his lifetime and after his death.

Queried on the collective’s claims, a representative for the Frida Kahlo Museum told ARTnews that, “In accordance with established protocols, the auction house Christie’s has been informed that the work is part of an ongoing investigation being conducted by the competent Mexican authorities.” It added, “An investigation file exists that gathers information on several works, including Congreso de los pueblos por la paz.”

According to the museum, INBAL “reported that, through its legal department, it has requested from Christie’s documentation proving the provenance and ownership of the painting.” Christie’s did not address whether it provided INBAL with the documentation in its statement to ARTnews.

A provenance published on Christie’s website, that has since been removed, listed the work’s earliest owner as Galería Ramis Barquet, a the Monterrey-based operation with a New York branch, run by Ramis Barquet, though it did not provide a date when Barquet came into possession of the work. An unnamed collector bought it from the gallery and put it up at auction at Sotheby’s in 2020. The current seller bought it at that sale for $2.6 million and is now consigning it to Christie’s.

INBAL did not respond to ARTnews’s request for comment by publication time. In a statement dated November 16 to the Mexican newspaper Excélsior, however, the institute said that Congress of the Peoples for Peace, “a painting created by Frida Kahlo in October 1952, was donated by the artist during her lifetime and left Mexico before the declaration of her work as an artistic monument.” It is unclear to whom Kahlo would have donated the work.

Kahlo painted Congreso de los pueblos por la paz two months before the Congress of the Peoples for Peace, which met in Vienna in December 1952. INBAL’s statement cited research from art historian Luis-Martín Lozano, who collaborated in cataloguing the painting for Christie’s. According to Lozano, Rivera took the painting to Vienna in late 1953, as recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s wife from 1955 until his death in 1957. The statement also pointed to Raquel Tibol’s 1977 book Frida Kahlo: Crónica, testimonios y aproximaciones, which reproduces the painting on plate 17.

In its statement, also from November 16, Defendamos la Colección Gelman disputed Lozano’s timeline of events. “The account—attributed to historian Luis-Martín Lozano—that the work was taken to the Congress in 1953 is chronologically impossible, as the Congress had already concluded months earlier. Furthermore, there is no evidence that Rivera returned to Europe that year; his travels were extensively documented—notably in the files that the FBI kept on him,” they wrote.

In its request for comment, ARTnews also asked INBAL about the discrepancy in Lozano’s research.

Furthermore, INBAL said that the export would not have covered Kahlo’s Congreso de los pueblos por la paz, claiming that it had left Mexico prior to July 25, 1984, when a decree declared her art an artistic monument and subject to Mexico’s strict cultural patrimony laws. Once designated “artistic monuments” of the nation, protected works may be bought and sold within Mexico but can leave the country only temporarily, unless INBAL grants an exceptional authorization.

“In previous cases, the INBAL has specified that the definitive export prohibition applies to works that were in national territory when the declaration of July 25, 1984 was published,” INBAL said.

After Kahlo’s death, Rivera notarized an inventory of the couple’s possessions as the basis for a trust administered by the Banco de México. The trust holds the properties and collections and oversees the reproduction rights to both artists’ work. Its proceeds were intended to support the upkeep of two museums: the Frida Kahlo Museum (Casa Azul) and the Museo Anahuacalli. It remains active today.

The inventory became the subject of public controversy in April 2025, when Hilda Trujillo, director of the Museo Anahuacalli and the Frida Kahlo Museum in Mexico City from 2002 to 2020, published a lengthy online post alleging that several works listed in Rivera’s inventory were currently unaccounted for. Among them, she wrote, was Congreso de los pueblos por la paz, which she said appears on Rivera’s list under the number A.F. 18. Defendamos la Colección Gelman provided ARTnews with a reproduction of the inventory including a zoomed-in, but blurry, image that reads, “18. – Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. – Oleo sobre masonite. – 1952. – 0.19 x 0.25.” (Christie’s lot entry gave the dimensions of the work as 18.7 x 24.8 centimeters.)

In her post, Trujillo traced the painting’s later whereabouts through a 2011 list that notes it as belonging to the collection of gallerist Mary-Anne Martin, and through the art historian Helga Prignitz-Poda’s 1988 catalogue raisonné, which attributed ownership to Barquet.

“It is unclear how or why it left the Frida Kahlo Museum,” she wrote. Trujillo accused the trust that manages both museums of mismanagement and negligence, claiming that in two episodes, in 2009 and 2013, its administrators dismissed evidence that works belonging to the Casa Azul may have been stolen and sold to private collectors in the United States. The trust responded to Trujillo’s allegations in a public statement that April that read in part: “The person making these accusations today never filed a formal complaint during their professional association with the trust.”

Defendamos la Colección Gelman described the case of Congreso de los pueblos por la paz as confirming “a troubling trend” that began with the Mexican government’s alleged lack of transparency surrounding the loan of the Gelman Collection to the new Faro Santander museum in Spain. “[W]hat once appeared to be an exception, the indefinite removal from the country of works designated as ‘Artistic Monuments’ with the consent of INBAL, is beginning to become the rule.”

The Gelman collection comprises more than 300 artworks, including a significant number of paintings by Kahlo and Rivera, as well as other important Mexican artists such as José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros.

item.title: Meet Natalie White, Photography’s Giant Polaroid Whisperer - Hyperallergic
item.description:
WHATELY, Mass. — The text message said to head around back to the barn, an only slightly ominous-looking structure with heavily weathered wooden siding, tucked off a winding road in Franklin County, Massachusetts. Inside was one of the world’s only 20x24 Polaroid Land Cameras — sometimes referred to as the Giant Polaroid — and the artist Natalie White, shooting with a rapidly dwindling stock of nearly 20-year-old film long past its expiration date.

A muse and model-turned-photographer, performance artist, and feminist activist, White just debuted 15 of her unique large-format Polaroids in Natalie White: Strange Magick, a selling exhibition at Phillips Los Angeles. The images are colorful and dreamy, close-up portraits of the artist with an otherworldly quality. Each photo is a double exposure, an unpredictable process that creates ghostly effects with White’s hands and fingers overlaid atop her face.

To achieve this, White leaves the film in the camera after pushing the shutter, takes a second shot, and hopes for the best. 

“We’re giving all control to the negative,” White told Hyperallergic. “We always joke that there’s a little magical man painting inside the camera who decides what the double exposure is going to look like.”

item.title: Esoteric Rituals Meet K-Pop in a Stop-Motion Music Video for Balming Tiger’s ‘Janjan’ - Colossal
item.description:
Deep in a phantasmagorical cave, a gathering of uncanny figures and critters emerges from dark waters in the music video for “Janjan” by alternative K-pop group Balming Tiger. Both playful and a little eerie, the animated work celebrates collectivity and freedom of expression.

Directed and animated by Takahashi Riku, a.k.a. DOKUZEN, the surreal music video is composed predominantly of stop-motion scenes set to a thumping rhythm to which fantastical paper figures dance as if performing esoteric rituals. It also features an interlude of drawn animations—a kind of world within a world.

item.title: Beer With a Painter: Ouattara Watts - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Last month, just a couple of weeks before Ouattara Watts’s solo show opened at Karma, I was directed to knock on the cracked glass door of his Bushwick studio. We met in the late afternoon, which is when his studio time begins. The Ivorian-American artist has coffee and a light evening meal, and works all night, before returning home to sleep during the day. To learn why Watts works only at night, one need only look at his paintings. He views art as a portal to the divine; night is when the veil with the spiritual realm is thinnest, and the outside voices of the physical world are quietest. 

Although a gallery representative had told me Watts would be putting “finishing touches” on the paintings for his exhibition at the time of our meeting, I came to realize that he thinks about the work, and his process, without a beginning or end. The centrifugal energy of his rhythmic compositions does not obey edges. Totemic forms continue beyond the bounds of the canvases; arrows point in varying directions; seed pods are split open to reveal concentric circles. His compositions are stained and dripped fields populated by a lexicon of imagery and symbols, developed over the past four decades. They include coffee beans, sacred books, musical notes, serpents, bursting petals encased in atoms, diagrammatic cubes, and mathematical codes.

item.title: Cologne Auction House Moves Forward with Sale of Gothic Paintings as Jewish Dealer’s Heirs Claim They Were ‘Stolen’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Cologne-based Lempertz auction house said it still planned to sell two works by Gothic painter Johann Koerbecke after the heirs of a German Jewish art dealer who was persecuted by the Nazis claimed the pieces were “stolen.”

Dealer Max Stern held the paintings in Düsseldorf between 1936 and 1937, the year the Nazis shut down his gallery. Per a provenance supplied by Lempertz, both paintings were then held by Düsseldorf’s Galerie Hans Bammann, which appears to have then sold them.

On Monday, the Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation issued a release in which it called on Lempertz to stop the sale of the two works planned for Saturday. According to the foundation, such a sale should not occur “until two distinct ownership claims of different victims are justly resolved according to the Washington Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art.”

Both paintings—The Annunciation and The Vision of Saint Bernard—are likely from Marienfeld high altarpiece, which was completed in 1457. They are being auctioned in a sale of Old Masters art. They carry high estimates of around 300,000 euros each, or about $329,000 apiece, making them the auction’s most expensive works. “For art historical reasons,” the Lempertz lot entries read, “the two important panels (Lots 1005 and 1006) will first be offered individually and then together.”

The Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation pointed out that both works appear in several databases of missing artworks, including the Interpol Database of Stolen Art since 2021. On the German Lost Art Database, both are reported as “Nazi-confiscated property”; the foundation registered that claim with the organization in 2018.

The foundation has demanded the return of multiple artworks belonging to Stern over the past decade, and in some cases, it has been successful. In 2017, for example, the FBI returned a painting by Jan Franse Verzijl that had been on view at an US art fair two years earlier.

Potentially complicating the matter is the fact that, prior to Stern’s possession of the Koerbecke paintings, they were owned by Ellen Funke, who, during the Nazi era, was classified as a Mischling, or “mongrel,” because she had Jewish ancestry through her mother. She sold her collection in 1936 to fund her emigration from Germany, and works she once owned have also been the subject of restitution claims—two of which happen to involve the Koerbecke works.

In 2025, Bavaria’s state museums restituted Koerbecke’s Vision of Saint Bernard to Funke’s heirs. At the time, the Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen noted that The Vision of Saint Bernard and The Annunciation were at one point part of a single work, with both images appearing on either side of the same panel, and that Stern had taken them apart with the hope of selling them both. Funke’s heirs are listed as the sellers of The Vision of Saint Bernard on the auction house’s website.

Similarly, Funke’s heirs are also listed as the sellers of the The Annunciation, which entered the Kolumba Art Museum of the Archdiocese of Cologne as a donation in 1996. The museum restituted the work in 2025.

The Dr. Max and Iris Stern Foundation’s release notably does not mention Funke by name. But it does state that the foundation “maintains that the rights and histories of both Jewish victims must be taken into account, and neither claim should be privileged at the expense of the other.” In an email to ARTnews, a spokesperson for the foundation said “the museums restituted the paintings to Ellen Funke’s heirs in accordance with the priority principle set forth in the guidelines established in Germany to apply the Washington Principles,” adding that that restitution ”did not result in a ‘just and fair solution’ in accordance with the Washington Principles.”

In a statement to ARTnews, Lempertz said it would not cancel its planned sale of the paintings by Koerbecke, who is widely considered one of the great painters of the Gothic era in Germany.

“We adhere to current restitution practices and follow the recommendations of the Federal Government,” a representative for the auction house said, claiming that the Stern “had the panels sawn in two” and went on to sell one of them for “double the price.”

“These magnificent paintings were not taken away from Max Stern,” the Lempertz representative said, adding, “Max Stern received compensation after the war; the heirs of the Funke family did not.”

The Stern Foundation spokesperson said the “view that the paintings were not ‘seized’ from Max Stern has long been refuted,” citing a 2019 statement from the now-defunct German Advisory Commission that the persecution of Jewish art dealers began at latest by August 1933, “so that from that point on at the latest, it can in no way be assumed that ‘proper, customary business transactions’ took place.” The spokesperson added that the claim that Max Stern was compensated for the paintings is “incorrect“ and has “no legal basis.”

Lempertz did not dispute the listings for both paintings on the Art Loss Register, but the representative also noted that the listings contain details of the works’ respective restitutions.

item.title: RIP to the National Historic Preservation Act - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the beloved American law that spent six decades giving communities a voice in federal decisions affecting the places that tell their stories, died shortly after its birthday following a brief but devastating bout of congressional malpractice. It was 60.

Born on October 15, 1966, with unanimous bipartisan support and signed into law by then-President Lyndon B. Johnson, NHPA was conceived in response to a national epidemic of federally sponsored demolition. Americans discovered that an astonishing 50% of the nation’s 12,000 historic buildings and landmarks documented in an inventory begun by the Civil Works Administration in 1933 had been demolished amid federally supported urban renewal and highway development — a breathtaking path of destruction dubbed “the death mask of America.”

NHPA’s central proposition was modest: Before the federal government or a developer damaged or destroyed an important part of America’s heritage, it simply needed to stop, look, and listen.

item.title: Sotheby’s, Blaquier-Arrieta Family Reach Deal With Fischer Heirs, Clearing Way for $180 M. Van Gogh Sale - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Sotheby’s has reached an agreement with the heirs of a Jewish publisher who challenged the sale of a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting last week, clearing the way for the picture to go under the hammer Wednesday night.

The auction house said Tuesday that the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) since 1975, reached a settlement with all the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer. The terms weren’t disclosed, but Sotheby’s confirmed to ARTnews that the agreement resolves the ownership claims and that the painting’s buyer will receive clear title.

The deal brings an end to a messy public brawl that erupted last Thursday in the pages of the New York Times, just six days before the painting was due to lead Sotheby’s $450 million sale of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection.

As the Times first reported, the Fischer heirs argued that their family had been forced to sell the painting in Amsterdam in 1936 because of financial pressures brought on by Nazi persecution. Their Berlin lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, demanded Sotheby’s withdraw the work from sale unless it could establish that the transaction had been voluntary.

Sotheby’s disputed that account. As ARTnews reported on Sunday the auction house said records from the archives of the art dealer Paul Cassirer showed that the painting sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, or approximately $22,000, in June 1936. Sotheby’s maintained that this was a fair price for a van Gogh at the time, and that the picture had been in Amsterdam for nearly three years before its sale.

The timing of the claim raised eyebrows among several art-market professionals who spoke to ARTnews under the condition of anonymity. Some saw it as a pressure tactic, arriving when Sotheby’s had little time to respond and plenty to lose if the picture was withdrawn. The auction house had guaranteed the work for an undisclosed sum and spent months promoting it as the star of one of the season’s biggest sales.

Judd Grossman, a New York art lawyer who isn’t involved in the dispute, warned that recent changes to the HEAR Act, which governs Nazi-era restitution claims, could encourage more of what he called “gamesmanship by claimants waiting to the very last minute to come forward before seeking their slice of the pie.” (As part of a separate ongoing lawsuit, lawyers for the Republic of Austria, the Albertina Museum, and the Leopold Museum Foundation have labeled the updated HEAR Act unconstitutional.)

Whether the Fischer heirs received any financial compensation under the agreement is unclear. Nor does the settlement establish whether the painting was sold under duress in 1936. In Tuesday’s announcement, Sotheby’s said the agreement recognized both the painting’s complicated history and the persecution suffered by the Fischer family under the Nazis.

The Fischer heirs welcomed the settlement, thanking Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family for what they called a “trusting and fair negotiation” that acknowledged their family’s suffering and honored Gisela Bermann Fischer’s long history of pursuing restitution.

Bermann Fischer, who died in 2014, had previously pursued restitution for artworks lost by her family during the Nazi era. In 2007, she declined to oppose the sale of a Paul Cezanne work that had passed through the same Amsterdam dealer, while expressly reserving her right to challenge other sales.

The Blaquier-Arrieta family also described the settlement positively, saying in a statement it looked forward to “an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”

item.title: Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, and Dawoud Bey Enter MCA Chicago Through 65-Work Gift - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago has received a promised gift of 65 artworks from longtime supporters Jack and Sandra Guthman to mark its 60th anniversary.

The gift from the Chicago-based collectors spans paintings, photography, works on paper, and sculptures, and includes works by Pope.L, Gary Simmons, Andrea Bowers, Christian Marclay, Elle Pérez, and Shinique Smith. The museum said in a release that the selected works were chosen in tandem with the curatorial staff, “taking the MCA’s collecting priorities into serious consideration.”

In its announcement, the MCA Chicago reported that, of the 54 artists represented in the gift, 23 (or 43 percent) are people of color, 19 (or 35 percente) are women, and 13 are entering the collection for the first time, among them Rashid Johnson, Christopher Wool, Dawoud Bey, and Amanda Williams. Johnson’s traveling survey, which opened at the Guggenheim Museum last year, is currently on view at the MCA Chicago; Williams will have a solo show at the museum next year.

“Together, Jack and Sandy have helped shape Chicago’s cultural life through their collecting, advocacy, and longstanding engagement with artists and institutions,” MCA Chicago director Madeleine Grynsztejn said in a statement. “To be entrusted with this tremendous gift is a great honor.”

The Guthmans first donated an artwork to the museum in 1988, and Jack joined the board of trustees the year after. To mark its 50th anniversary in 2016, they donated work by 50 women-identifying photographers, which was the subject of the exhibition “Woman With a Camera.” With the newly donated 65 works, the Guthmans have given a total of 130 works over the past nearly four decades, the largest amount by a single collector in the MCA Chicago’s history.

Jack is an attorney who has worked on several mega-developments in Chicago. He is also the founder and past board chair of the Chicago Architecture Biennial. Sandra worked at IBM from 1965 to 1993, rising from systems engineer to director of marketing for the Midwest. She also served as chief executive and chair of the Chicago-based Polk Bros. Foundation; she is now chair emerita. In addition to the MCA Chicago, they have supported the Art Institute of Chicago, the Hyde Park Art Center, Theaster Gates’s Art Bank, and the Harris Theater for Music and Dance. At the Harris, they sponsored the creation of the Guthman Gallery.

Last month, the MCA Chicago received a $5 million gift from the Bluhm family to endow the Women Artists Initiative, which will provide funds in perpetuity to help the museum achieve its gender equity goals in its programming and collection. Both gifts are meant to honor Grynsztejn, who is stepping down at the end of the year.

“We are fortunate to have the opportunity to donate these works as the MCA marks its 60th anniversary and as Madeleine Grynsztejn steps down after a remarkable tenure as its Pritzker Director,” the Guthmans said in a statement. “We celebrate both the institution and the woman who has lifted it to a where it is today—a Chicago institution now acknowledged as a leader in the world of contemporary art.”

item.title: Artsy and Artnet Acquire First Thursday as Art-Tech Expansion Picks Up Speed - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Artsy and Artnet have another deal: The two art-market platforms announced the acquisition of First Thursday, a London-based startup that uses artificial intelligence to help galleries keep track of collectors, manage relationships, and, ideally, sell more art.

The purchase comes seven months after Artsy and Artnet joined forces under Beowolff Capital, the investment firm founded by Andrew Wolff. And just last week, Artnet announced a partnership with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that allows users to bet on auction results, prompting a rather unenthusiastic response from parts of the art world.

The latest deal, whose financial terms weren’t disclosed, is a little less controversial. It also gives a clearer picture of what the combined company is trying to build: a single system that galleries can use to manage almost every part of their businesses.

Founded in 2023 by Callum Hale-Thomson, First Thursday specializes in what it calls “collector intelligence.” In practice, that means gathering years of emails, sales records, inquiries, and notes into one searchable place, then using AI to help dealers figure out which collectors might be interested in a particular work.

Hale-Thomson, whose parents are both artists, told ARTnews that the idea came to him after he spent six months working inside London galleries, effectively serving as their IT guy and watching how they operated. He found that many were sitting on years of valuable information without an easy way to use it.

“You’re sitting on an unbelievable trove of information,” he said, describing the emails, notebooks, and other records galleries accumulate over time. The problem was finding anything useful when it was needed.

First Thursday’s existing software helps with that. At an art fair, for example, a dealer can scan a visitor’s business card, record which painting caught their eye, and send a follow-up email directly from thier phone. The system can also bring together past correspondence and publicly available information about collectors, helping galleries identify potential buyers they might otherwise have overlooked.

Under the new ownership, Hale-Thomson and his team will help develop a broader gallery-management platform, scheduled to launch for select Artsy and Artnet partners in early 2027. It will combine collector records with inventory management, sales tools, invoicing, marketing, and online viewing rooms. Galleries will also be able to publish works to Artsy and Artnet directly from the system.

The initial focus will be smaller galleries, which often lack the money or staff to maintain sophisticated software.

Alex Forbes, who oversees global partnerships for Artsy and Artnet, told ARTnews that the smallest gallery partners will be able to use the core system without paying more than they already do for their Artsy subscriptions.

Larger galleries will be able to purchase additional features and access for bigger teams. Exact pricing will be announced when the platform launches.

“We want it to be the easiest to start out with for a small gallery,” Forbes said, while also making it useful for businesses with more complicated operations.

The move takes Artsy and Artnet further into a competitive market for gallery software, where established companies such as Artlogic already offer inventory and business-management tools. Last year, Artlogic merged with ArtCloud, another sign of consolidation in the art-tech business. (Artsy is already integrated with Artlogic and Artcloud, which, according to an Artsy spokesperson, the company will continue to support.)

Forbes acknowledged that galleries have different needs and that no single product will necessarily suit everyone. But he said the broader plan is to connect the company’s existing marketplaces and pricing data with the software that galleries use to run their businesses.

One potentially sensitive question is what happens to all that collector information. Artsy and Artnet say galleries will retain control of their data, which will remain private unless they choose to share it with the platforms.

For Hale-Thomson, who will remain with the business, the opportunity is to bring more sophisticated tools to galleries that haven’t traditionally been able to afford them.

And for Artsy and Artnet, the acquisition marks another step toward becoming something considerably bigger than two websites where people look at art, check prices, and occasionally buy something. Increasingly, they want to provide the software that keeps the business running.

item.title: Latinx Art’s New Visionaries - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Optimism is a rare sight in this day and age — which is why scholar Arlene Dávila’s unabashed excitement about Latinx art right now is so invigorating. These artists draw from vernacular traditions, community histories, family memories, and more to reframe the narrative, despite facing a barrage of attacks in recent years. “The work of these new visionaries is a rallying cry,” she writes in an opinion piece today. “Now is the time to write, create, and make art boldly — together.”

Read on for a pulse on the rest of the art world, from novelist Stephanie Wambugu on Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, to Martin Puryear’s quietly revolutionary sculptures, to a new film reevaluating Frida Kahlo’s legacy and commodification. And it wouldn’t be the art world without some auction drama. Today, heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer call on Sotheby’s to withdraw a Van Gogh painting it valued at $180 million, alleging that the work was sold under duress during World War II. Meanwhile, at Christie’s, a Willem de Kooning painting that entered the Whitney’s collection just a few years ago is headed under the hammer as Marquee Week kicks off in NYC.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Latinx Artists Are the New Visionaries

Latinx communities are facing one of the most aggressive series of attacks in recent history, with many families enduring the pain of separation, persecution, and dehumanization. But if you’ve been paying attention to Latinx arts and culture, you’ll see that as we are being told to hide and disappear, artists are stepping into newfound confidence, showcasing the full value and complexity of our identities. | Arlene Dávila

item.title: At Sotheby’s $378.7 M. Doubleheader, Buyers Take Risks Again, Even as Bidding Drags - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Sotheby’s kicked off the November marquee sales with a doubleheader on Monday evening that generated $378.7 million across 74 lots. The top-line results look solid, but a sluggish second half seemed to further illustrate the choosy mood among collectors right now.

The nearly three-hour marathon started strong with the dedicated sale from the collection of cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum. It was a white-glove result, with all 24 works sold for a hammer total of $90.9 million. With fees, the sale landed at $110 million, just a shade above the presale high estimate of $109 million.

The Baum sale was a lively affair from the start. After the first lot—Roy Lichtenstein’s 1983 cut-paper work Two Paintings: Sleeping Muse (Study)—sparked a four-minute contest among three specialists and a bidder in the room, CEO Charles Stewart strode over to Gareth Jones, the house’s chief marketing officer, and said of the $3.8 million total, “Well, that’s a good start.” Three lots later, a Lucio Fontana copper canvas with a glorious cut down the middle ignited another bidding war, the bids ricocheting among three bidders in the room. It hammered at $3.5 million, or $4.4 million with fees, well above the $3 million high estimate.

Oliver Barker, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, handled the proceedings with panache, making even a fairly ordinary stretch of bidding feel brisk. Amid the bidding for Lot 7, Andy Warhol’s 1984 painting The Scream (After Munch), he teased Jacqueline Wachter, chairwoman of private sales, for taking a bit too long with her phone bidder, asking whether she was “doing her shopping or doing her conversions.” Then he quipped to the audience, “Amazon is always open. As is Sotheby’s Dot Com.” It was a little sharp, perhaps, but it got a laugh and helped lighten the mood as the sale began to drag.

The crowded salesroom was a who’s who of the art trade: Dominique Lévy, Brett Gorvy, Amalia Dayan, David Schrader, Emmanuel Di Donna, Christophe Van de Weghe, and Gagosian Art Advisory’s Bernard Lagrange were just a few of the heavies in attendance.

In the end, six works hammered above their estimates and another 10 landed in range, with spirited bidding throughout, both in the room and on the phone. Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest led the sale at $19.3 million, followed by Mark Rothko’s Untitled at $17.7 million and Ed Ruscha’s Dimple at $11.6 million. The Baums had bought the Mitchell privately in 1986 for just $65,000, making its sale price nearly 300 times what they paid. The Rothko, which they acquired for $115,000 in 1983, brought more than 150 times its purchase price. Not bad for a few decades of collecting. The final lot in the sale, Mario Merz’s neon sculpture Iguana, sold well below its estimate, but that did little to dampen the enthusiasm, as the room erupted in applause.

The Now and Contemporary sale that followed was considerably less celebratory. Of the 53 lots originally offered, three were withdrawn before the sale, and another five went unsold: works by Kerry James Marshall, Ellsworth Kelly, Roy Lichtenstein, and Keith Haring, and, curiously, a Formula One race car. Tom Eddison, head of contemporary art at Sotheby’s London, who took over auctioneering duties for the sale, said the car was a first for the auction house, and it required a lengthy preamble explaining that the sale was subject to the terms of service of RM Sotheby’s, the house’s classic-car affiliate. The car garnered a handful of bids but failed to reach its low estimate before Eddison declared it unsold. It may be some time before Sotheby’s tries that experiment again.

That’s not to say the results for the contemporary sale were lackluster. When all was said and done, the sale garnered a hammer total of $224.8 million. With fees, the total climbed to $268.8 million, within the presale aggregate estimate of $226.2 million to $323 million, and well above the equivalent sale in November 2025, which generated $178.5 million. Of course, we should note that last year’s sale followed the trove of works from the late cosmetics heir Leonard Lauder, which generated an eye-watering $527.5 million. Alas, not every season sees three Klimts hit the block.

Of the 45 lots that sold, a full 14 hammered above their presale estimates, and another 24 landed in range. Still, while there always seemed to be a handful of bidders for each sold lot, with Eddison darting his hands left, right, and center, most works hammered after only a minute or two.

The most protracted bidding wars came somewhat early. A six-minute contest among four specialists for Jeff Koons’s 1991 sculpture Bob-Tail ended with contemporary art specialist Bame Fierro March winning the lot for a hammer price of $9 million. At $10.7 million with fees, that’s good for just over three times the high estimate. (Is Koons’s market trending back up, or do collectors just really like an adorable English sheepdog?) Seven lots later, Agnes Martin’s cream canvas Desert, from the collection of Lenore and Bernard Greenberg, sold after a six-minute duel between contemporary art specialist Alya Sama and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas. Dennison won on a $9.2 million hammer bid, or $11.3 million with fees, comfortably above the $8 million high estimate. And Andy Warhol’s 1964–65 painting Flowers fetched $18.2 million with fees against a $10 million to $15 million estimate.

Mark the Warhol and Koons results as green shoots for a market that’s spent much of the past two years playing it safe. Neither artist has had the easiest time in the secondary market lately, which makes those results particularly interesting. Something to watch going forward, especially for Koons.

After the sale, Dennison pointed to the continued strength of early Martin paintings, which have been outperforming expectations for several seasons.

Art adviser Ed Dolman similarly found the night’s results encouraging. In a text message toward the end of the sale, he said, “The best works always do fine, [but] buyers were taking some risks again.”

Dolman also pointed to the depth of bidding. While 29 of the 45 sold lots in the contemporary sale had guarantees—as did every work in the Baum sale—those guarantors were often outbid on Monday night. Buyers, it seemed, were willing to go a little further.

Not that everything was suddenly flying off the walls. Lichtenstein’s Reflections on ‘Painter and Model,’ the top lot of the contemporary sale at $24.7 million with fees, came in well short of the high end of its $20 million to $30 million estimate. Willem de Kooning’s Water…Soft Banks of a Window (Untitled VIII) brought $20.3 million, just above its $20 million low estimate, while Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I made $17.1 million against a $15 million to $20 million estimate.

The buzziest result of the night was no doubt for Yayoi Kusama’s 1960 painting No. 3P.B., which hammered for $12.5 million after 10 bids spread across four minutes. With fees, the result came to $15.1 million, just above the $15 million high estimate, and good for a new record for the artist, who died in August. About 10 lots later, another of her “Infinity Nets” paintings, Infinity Nets (OZEH), sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.1 million with fees, just a shade above the $3 million high estimate. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011. And if you missed out on those two Kusamas, have no fear: Another 10 works of hers will hit the block over the rest of marquee week. Five are from her long-running “Infinity Nets” series.

Yet, for all the strong prices, the second half of the contemporary sale was a slog. With Eddison at the rostrum, the pace slowed considerably. Bids were drawn out, pauses stretched on, and even works that eventually fetched impressive prices seemed to take an age to get there. A few market watchers wondered whether such a sluggish tempo might discourage bidders, particularly on works that didn’t have much competition to begin with. It was an odd contrast: a sale that sometimes felt as though it was struggling to find its rhythm, even as buyers were spending millions more than expected.

To Nina Del Rio, an art adviser and auction house veteran, the results looked remarkably strong, particularly given the subdued energy in the second half of the sale. Still, she said, there hasn’t been much evidence of a shift in the market. At least not a fundamental one. Buyers appear to be behaving much as they did in May, when the best works attracted serious money but enthusiasm for younger artists remained muted. A few years ago, the Now sale was where collectors went to get their hands on artists whose waiting lists seemed impossible to crack. That sense of urgency has largely disappeared.

What collectors do seem willing to pay for is scarcity. Del Rio pointed to the modern masterpieces coming up later in the week, the sort of works that rarely appear at auction and may not come around again for decades. Among them is Wednesday’s sale of the Blaquier Collection, a group of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces said to be worth around $450 million, and a $180 million Van Gogh suddenly subject to a last-minute restitution claim.

Dennison warned against reading too much into a single evening. Given the current mood, starting the week with contemporary art rather than a mix of modern and contemporary masterpieces makes it harder to judge the market as a whole. And while works in the $10 million to $20 million range performed well, the sale lacked the $30 million, $40 million, and $50 million trophies that drive enthusiasm across the whole week.

As for that Formula One car, Dennison said the result left her scratching her head. The last bid offered, $3.9 million, was just under the $4 million low estimate. Did the interested buyer really think the $100,000 gap was too wide to bridge?

There is a risk to putting something unexpected into a contemporary art sale. But, as Dennison pointed out, sometimes it works, as when Christie’s sold the Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton “Stan” during its 20th Century Evening Sale in 2020 for $31.8 million, nearly quadruple the high estimate.

Sotheby’s shouldn’t give up on the idea. There’s something appealing about an evening sale that doesn’t draw a firm boundary around paintings and sculptures. Not every experiment works the first time, or even the second. And if the object is truly one-of-a-kind, buyers are ready to shell out the cash.

item.title: Yayoi Kusama ‘Infinity Net’ Painting Sells for $15.1 M. at Sotheby’s, Setting a Record - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Just months after Yayoi Kusama’s death, one of her paintings sold at Sotheby’s New York on Monday night for a hammer price of $12.5 million, or $15.1 million with fees, setting a new auction record for the artist.

The work sold after a brief bidding war between Evelyn Lin, chairman of modern and contemporary art, Asia, and Lisa Dennison, chairman of the Americas, both of whom were bidding on behalf of clients on the phone. Lin ultimately prevailed after 10 bids over the course of four minutes. The $12.5 million hammer price placed the work squarely within its presale estimate of $10 million to $15 million.

No. 3P.B. (1960), is one of Kusama’s “Infinity Net” paintings, a series of large-scale monochrome abstractions in which the canvas is covered with thousands of looping brushstrokes. Kusama painted her first “Infinity Net” work in 1958, shortly after moving from Japan to New York, which makes No. 3P.B. a rare early example of the form. The crimson canvas, which stands more than five feet tall, appeared in the Whitney Museum’s 1961 painting-focused annual exhibition, a precursor to the Whitney Biennial.

About 10 lots later on Monday night, another painting from the series, Infinity Nets (OZEH), sold for a hammer price of $2.5 million, or $3.06 million with fees. That work, a white canvas measuring roughly 6½ by 8½ feet, is far more recent, dating to 2011.

Like Kusama’s “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” which are more popular on social media, the “Infinity Net” series deals with obsession and repetition. The series is often said to prefigure the Minimalism and Post-Minimalism of the 1960s and 1970s, and it made her name in a male-dominated art world. Reviewing the paintings for ARTnews in 1959, Donald Judd wrote, “The expression transcends the question of whether it is Oriental or American. Although it is something of both, certainly of such Americans as Rothko, Still and Newman, it is not at all a synthesis and is thoroughly independent.”

Since Kusama died in August at 97, nearly 30 of her works have come to auction at Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips. The top results have been for two paintings of pumpkins, another of her signature motifs. At Sotheby’s Hong Kong in September, the 2010 painting Pumpkin (TWPOT) sold for HK$60.7 million, or about $7.74 million. The next day at Christie’s Hong Kong, the 2011 painting A-Pumpkin (YHP), which shows a yellow pumpkin on a patterned black background, sold for HK$58.2 million, or about $7.43 million.

Besides No. 3P.B., 11 more Kusama works will go on the block this week. Five of them are “Infinity Net” paintings, but none is nearly as early or as highly valued.

Kusama’s previous auction record was set in 2022 at Phillips New York by the 1959 painting Untitled (Nets), 1959, a white “Infinity Net” made a year before No. 3P.B. It sold for $10.5 million with fees.

item.title: Who Sat for Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait? A New Catalog Essay Suggests It May Have Been the Artist - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The catalog for the exhibition “Van Eyck: The Portraits” opening at London’s National Gallery on November 21, has reignited a long-standing debate about the identity of couple in the Early Netherlandish master’s mysterious Arnolfini Portrait (1434). As reported in the Art Newspaper, one of the catalog’s essays suggests that the man in the painting, usually identified as a member of the Arnolfini family of Italian merchants, is in fact Jan van Eyck himself.

In the painting, which is owned by the National Gallery and a centerpiece of the show, an elegantly dressed man and woman pose hand in hand in a private room. Every item in the chamber, including the couple’s fur-trimmed clothing, the oriental carpet on the floor, and even the orange resting on a windowsill—an expensive luxury at the time—signals understated wealth.

The man and the woman are clearly husband and wife, though the work does not, as was once believed, depict a marriage ceremony. A 16th-century inventory of the holdings of Margaret of Austria, the painting’s owner at the time, identifies it as “Hernoul le Fin” or “Arnoult Fin,” which is widely interpreted by art historians as “Arnolfini.”

Scholars have disagreed however, however, about which Arnolfini the man in the painting might be. Possible candidates are either Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (though recent discoveries suggest he was not married at the time the painting was made), or more likely his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, who would have been in his late thirties in 1434.

Giovanni’s first wife Costanza Trenta died in 1433; thus, according to the National Gallery’s website, the woman is probably his second wife, whose identity is unknown. Alternatively, as art historian Margaret Koster and others have suggested, the painting may be a memorial piece.

It is also possible that the sitters were friends of Van Eyck’s. Reflected in the convex mirror behind them, two more men can be seen entering the room. Prominently written on the wall above the mirror is the inscription “Johannes de Eyck fuit hic. 1434” (“Jan van Eyck was here. 1434”), which is sometimes taken to mean that the men in the mirror are Van Eyck and his servant arriving for a visit.

But Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in one of the catalog’s essays, asserts instead that the subjects of the painting are Van Eyck and his wife Margaret. Kemperdick is a curator at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which owns several Van Eycks, including Portrait of a Man in a Red Chaperon (1390–1440/41) of the same man in the Arnolfini Portrait at an older age. He bases his theory on the inscription’s placement in the Arnolfini Portrait next to the male figure’s head, arguing that this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man.

If true, Kemperdick’s theory would throw the identification of the subjects in other Van Eyck paintings into doubt. The National Gallery’s Portrait of a Man (1433), of a much older man than the man in the Arnolfini Portrait, is currently tentatively identified as a self-portrait, while the entry for the Berlin work—Kemperdick’s theory notwithstanding—still notes that it is presumed to be of Giovanni Arnolfini. (Both Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) and Portrait of a Man in a Red Chaperon (Giovanni Arnolfini?) are included in the exhibition, which brings together all nine of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.)

For his part, Nicholas Flory, the exhibition’s co-curator along with Emma Capron, told the Art Newspaper that he found Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative.” He notes that the sitter in another work in the show from the Musea Brugge, definitively known to be of Margaret based on an inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

German art historian Till-Holger Borchert, the former director of the Musea Brugge—concurs, finding the 16th-century inventory reference near conclusive proof that the painting is of an Arnolfini. But, he added, given how little is known about Van Eyck’s life, “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”

item.title: Why Is the Whitney Museum Selling a De Kooning Painting? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Looking to cash in on marquee week in New York, the Whitney Museum of American Art has consigned a Willem de Kooning painting from its collection to Christie's for its 20th-century evening sale tomorrow, November 17. Once a promised gift to the museum, de Kooning's “Yellow River” (1958) is expected to fetch up to $18 million.

The practice of museum deaccessioning has long been a subject of controversy. In 2022, the Association of Art Museum Directors (AAMD) loosened its policy to allow institutions to apply funds from the sale of deaccessioned art toward the “direct care” of their collections.

A lot description for “Yellow River” on Christie's website notes that the proceeds will benefit the Whitney's collection. The Whitney has not yet responded to Hyperallergic's request for comment, but a museum spokesperson told Artnet News that deaccessioning is “a component of the Whitney’s collections strategic plan, allowing the museum to thoughtfully evaluate and refine its holdings in support of its long-term collection priorities.”

The de Kooning painting going under that hammer had a rooted connection to the Whitney before it was bequeathed to the museum in 2023. Postwar art collector, attorney, and museum trustee David Solinger, who would go on to become the museum's first president beyond the Whitney family in 1966, purchased the work from de Kooning's sold-out exhibition at Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959.

“Yellow River” emerged from a series of “highway" paintings representing the artist's shift from cacophonous urban compositions to more airy landscapes, designating the freeway as a conduit connecting New York City to the Hudson River Valley and Long Island's South Fork. In vibrant warm yellow, earthy brown tones, and stretches of deep blue, de Kooning's decisive gestures direct viewers across overlapping paths and visual rest stops throughout the canvas.

“I love to be on those highways,” de Kooning said to British critic and curator David Sylvester about the expansive roads during a BBC interview in 1960. “And they are really not very pretty, but the big embankments and the shoulders of the roads and the curves are flawless.”

“Yellow River” hung at the foot of Solinger's bed for some time, serving as a testament to Solinger's fascination with the artist. His wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, took ownership of the work after Solinger passed in 1996, and in 2011, she designated the work as a promised gift to the Whitney in honor of her late husband. It officially entered the Whitney's holdings in 2023, the same year that the museum deaccessioned seven works, including an Edward Hopper landscape, and sent them to auction to benefit the collection.

item.title: Talking Art and Data With Mona Chalabi - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
