item.title: What Mary Lovelace O'Neal Left Behind - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Upon her death in May 2026, the abstract painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal left behind a monumental body of work. Her oeuvre includes signature large blackened canvases, marked by fluid, ecstatic gestures in neon paint that resemble the glowing afterimages of a moving flame. O’Neal’s first posthumous exhibition, Requiem, is a fitting self-elegy for the painter precisely because nothing about it feels mournful. 

The work could not be more vital, and in it one feels the artist’s energetic and intuitive handling of paint as a kind of physical charge. O’Neal’s compositions transmit a powerful sense of presence and force, as though inviting viewers into the vicarious experience of an artist grappling with the formal concerns of color and line before transcending them.

The result is an almost oceanic feeling, one I imagine is equally profound in the making of a painting as staggering as the intense, cascading standout “Requiem for a Daffodil” (1997). The black, fingerlike marks that protrude from the surrounding deep navy seem to be reaching for the floral clusters and reeds in the painting’s top half, like a perpetual grasping at splendor in the shadows. 

Though non-representational, these works continually approach figuration, filled with partial outlines of human and animal forms. These half-figures peer through their dark surroundings, like the pink mass in the center of “What’s Time to a Pig” (c. 1990s), and are caught in a constant state of emergence. Like an act of divine creation, O’Neal captures the transformation of raw material into something seemingly miraculous through the hands of a master craftsman. 

During this formative and fruitful period between the 1970s and 1990s, when her visual language and iconoclastic artistic sensibility crystallized, O’Neal was also coming into her own as an artist. She was a groundbreaking student, becoming the first Black woman to receive an MFA from Columbia University in 1969, and in 1985, she became the first African American professor to receive tenure in UC Berkeley’s Department of Art Practice. 

The back room offers a rich sketch of the painter’s life as it intersected with both world history and art history. Born in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1942, Jim Crow was fully in place in the American South during the artist’s childhood.  She attended Howard University in 1960 alongside David Driskell and Lois Mailou Jones, dated the activist Stokely Carmichael, and was an activist in her own right. 

The archival materials reveal the cultural and political concerns of O’Neal’s time. It’s all the more remarkable that she navigated these constraints while retaining the verve and genuine, delightful strangeness these paintings must have necessitated. “Untitled” (n.d.) gets at the humor and irreverence of O’Neal’s style. An Uncle Sam-like figure, half-covered in chalky white paint, evokes a satirical Ralph Bakshi cartoon, with many identifying features erased. It has a winking quality. Though political in nature, it foregrounds O’Neal’s formal concerns, which circle mainly around the possibilities of certain pigments (like the enveloping darkness of lampblack contrasted with punchy neons) and the permeable boundary between abstraction and figuration. It is this formal rigor that made O’Neal trailblazing in more ways than one –– both as a Black American shattering institutional barriers and as a woman painter making important interventions into the inherited, lionized artistic movements of the Color Field, Abstract Expressionism, and Minimalism. 

“Race Woman Series #7” (1992–93) dramatizes the tension between the structural or compositional and the political, suggesting that it was an enduring preoccupation for the artist. A dazed face vaguely springs up from a prominent green being, which could just be read as an indecipherable scrawl, while a white specter at the top of the canvas drips over it. O’Neal’s use of color is frenetic and instinctive, resulting in a painting that is too varied to slot into a clear interpretation. Like the Klannish chiaroscuro of Norman Lewis’ “Alabama” (1960), the legibility of “Race Woman Series #7” relies on the light its instructive title sheds on it. 

But unlike Lewis, when we search for correlation between O’Neal’s caption and the canvas, we are pulled deeper into her self-reflexive, numinous and unrepeatable idiom, which makes its own intuitive sense and, anyway, seeks to go beyond sense-making into the terrain of near-mystical experience. 

Mary Lovelace O’Neal: Requiem continues at Boesky Gallery (509 West 24th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan) through December 19. The exhibition is organized by the gallery.

item.title: What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
These days, Frida Kahlo isn’t free. She is the plastic cosmetic bag in an Ulta carousel. She is a throw pillow in a World Market bin. Her name and image might be the most commodified of the 20th century, so ubiquitous that she feels emptied of meaning. Or is she?

Relying primarily on the testimony of Mexican voices, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, a new documentary by Trisha Ziff, poses this question across a colorful spectrum of socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. “I learned about Communism from Frida’s bookshelf,” shares actress and activist Ofelia Medina, who visited Kahlo’s home on a sixth-grade field trip.

“Frida gave me strength, she gave me a life and a job,” explains Juana López Sánchez, an Indigenous artisan whose livelihood is selling hand-crafted Frida dolls in Mexico City.

item.title: Video Artist Pipilotti Rist Wins MIT’s $100,000 Arts Award - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Pipilotti Rist, one of the most widely acclaimed living video artists, has another feather in her cap in the form of next year’s Eugene McDermott Award in the Arts, a prize given out by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology that comes with $100,000 and a residency on campus.

The Swiss artist is known for phantasmagoric installations that have harnessed video technology to explore the human body in all its many forms. Often working with a heavy dose of humor, Rist has thoughtfully used her camera to explore sexuality, sleep states, and the female form.

Today, she is perhaps best known for her 1997 video installation Ever Is Over All, in which a woman walks down a city street and smashes in car windows with flowers. The work was memorably retooled in the visual album for Beyoncé’s Lemonade.

“I am kissing your Institute and your feet,” Rist said in a statement about the MIT award. “I am immensely touched and grateful to have this trust and investment in ideas I’ve yet to conceive. I’m honored to receive an award that has been granted to so many of my heroes, and look forward to collaborating closely with the brilliant minds at MIT.”

Her past achievements include representing Switzerland at the Venice Biennale in 2005 and a retrospective that appeared at New York’s New Museum in 2016. According to the website for Hauser & Wirth, the mega-gallery that represents her alongside New York’s Luhring Augustine, Rist will stage a permanent installation at the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi when it opens in December.

item.title: Martin Puryear’s Liberatory Violence - Hyperallergic
item.description:
ATLANTA — Despite my best efforts to be anything else, I am a writer, and not even the Marines-like insanity of Bard’s interdisciplinary MFA or my day job in the library could erase that from me. Every object instantly becomes a word I see on a perfectly white page, a symbol made up of assorted shapes like “bicycle” (object that carried me from my home to the High Museum of Art) or “press pass” (object that allows me into the High Museum of Art), a compulsion that is always at its worst when viewing sculpture in the page-white tomb of a museum.

I was grateful for that compulsion, however, when I viewed Martin Puryear’s Nexus. Writing, underneath its surface, is extremely violent, exceptionally bloody, and annihilatory in scope. It is almost impossible to describe the reality of this fact on the page, and I have struggled even further to articulate this vocally to others, even other writers. So when walking into Nexus and “Bask” (1976) was there, lying as still and deadly as a knife on its white plinth, I smiled in surprised relief and my body physically relaxed. Puryear is noted for his use of natural materials — wood, rawhide, fiber — and his attention to traditional practices like basket weaving, boatmaking, tanning, and structure building from peoples around the world, which obscures the sculptures’ violence under that tricky word, “natural.”

item.title: Restitution Claim on $180M Van Gogh Shakes Up Sotheby's Marquee Week - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Heirs of a prominent Jewish publishing family have called on Sotheby's to withdraw a rare Vincent van Gogh painting highlighted in the marquee auction sales in New York City this week, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe.

The heirs allege that the family member who owned the painting, which Sotheby's valued at a record-breaking $180 million, sold it because of Nazi-imposed restrictions on what emigrant Jews were allowed to take with them at the time.

Sotheby's confirmed to Hyperallergic that the painting is still slated to go under the hammer this Wednesday, November 18, and that it was aware of the heirs' concerns and “takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the [painting's] ownership history.”

item.title: Vienna Museum’s Mummified Remains Reveal Cats Lived and Died Brutally in Ancient Egypt - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Cats in ancient Egypt may have endured nine exceptionally hard lives, according to findings related to feline skulls in the collection of the Natural History Museum in Vienna.

As reported by Popular Mechanics, research on 131 skulls from a funerary site in Middle Egypt led by zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences revealed “disturbing” evidence that the cats may have been killed for the sake of offerings to the goddess known as Bastet. “Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma,” the report reads. “Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.”

It gets worse: “The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today.”

The research, published in the Journal of Archaeological Science, also shared grim news regarding the manner in which the killed cats met their ends. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers said. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”

item.title: The Poignant Animation ‘Paper Trail’ Chronicles a Life in Handwriting - Colossal
item.description:
From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by Don Hertzfeldt, the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school. We witness his cursive lessons and adolescent love letters to a girl named Lindsey before observing grocery lists and remnants of his professional life.

Based in Austin, Texas, Hertzfeldt is known for his poetic animations that harness the indelible intimacy of hand-drawn scenes. “Paper Trail” has been on the festival circuit where it’s garnered top honors at Annecy, Sundance, SXSW, and many others. The film is available for streaming for a limited-timed on Vimeo, along with more of Hertzfeldt’s work.

item.title: Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LONDON — In Paris, in the years leading up to the massive social upheavals of 1968, Julio Le Parc was making the first of his Game Rooms. These were collections of works that aimed to playfully destabilize the viewer’s experience, such as seats with springs that challenged the act of sitting, areas of uneven tile floors, and patterned discs designed to be manually spun. But for Le Parc, as well as the progressive collective Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) that he co-founded, the works were about far more than entertainment. Indeed, he hoped that cultivating the audience’s active participation would not only disrupt what he saw as the hierarchical and passive nature of the museum, but also effect a political awakening outside of it.

A recreation of one of the Game Rooms appears in the exhibition Julio Le Parc: Light. Colour. Action., which was “developed in close dialogue with the artist,” before his death earlier this year at the age of 97. Though the current world, as in 1960s Paris, grapples with mounting social and political tensions, one is unlikely to describe today’s art museum experience as “passive.” Indeed, outgoing Tate Modern Interim Director Catherine Wood notes in the exhibition catalog’s foreword, “At a time of heightened popularity for exhibitions touting immersive and interactive experiences, celebrating Julio Le Parc’s seven-decade career with a monographic exhibition at Tate Modern feels especially meaningful and urgent.”

item.title: Draconian Trump Executive Order Could Strip Art Orgs of Nonprofit Status - Hyperallergic
item.description:
After the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that the White House is considering an executive order that would strip nonprofits deemed to have alleged "terrorist ties" of their tax-exempt status, many arts and culture organizations are bracing for what could be a series of politically targeted attacks from the Trump administration.

According to the report, officials are reviewing Section 501(p)(2)(C) of the United States Internal Revenue Code, which authorizes the president to label nonprofits that are allegedly "supporting or engaging in terrorist activity." Organizations tagged with the label would have their tax-exempt status immediately suspended, spelling a potentially devastating blow to their operations.

The White House has not made an official confirmation or announcement of the measure, with a spokesperson telling Hyperallergic that "any policy announcements will come directly from the President," and "discussions about potential decisions or their impacts are otherwise baseless speculation."

item.title: From Pipe Cleaners to Clay, Baskets Break Craft Traditions in ‘Interwoven’ - Colossal
item.description:
Conjure an image of a basket in your mind. Is it made of straw, or perhaps sweetgrass or willow? Does it have a handle? Was it made by hand, and what could it hold? At Mindy Solomon Gallery, a forthcoming exhibition titled Interwoven: Basketry As Expanded Practice challenges our perception of both object and craft.

Curated by Dee Clements, the exhibition considers the way basketmaking techniques are far from limited to the splinted white ash trug we might carry out to the garden or the simple vessel that holds recipes in the kitchen. This vibrant survey “breaks craft tradition,” Clements says, positioning the practice as an art form. The show asks “what happens when basketry is understood not as a fixed category of craft, but as an open-ended artistic language?”

The artists in Interwoven use a range of materials, from ceramic and steel to cotton and paper. Salvador Dominguez’s vibrant pipe cleaner vessels are complemented by wall works like Eric Gushee’s intricately interlaced wire sculptures and Miguel Arzabe’s woven, deconstructed paintings.

Viewers will find further explorations by artists like Dienke Dekker and José Santiago Pérez, who work with unexpected materials like paper and emergency blankets, respectively. And Colossal readers might also recognize work by Xanthe Somers and Sonia Barrett, among the nearly two dozen participating artists.

Interwoven opens on November 29 and continues through January 9 in Miami. See more on the gallery’s Instagram.

item.title: Hockney and His Beverly Hills Patron - Hyperallergic
item.description:
It’s a beautiful day to support indie publications! Last week, a survey conducted by Critical Minded and the Rabkin Foundation quantified the precarity of independent US-based art magazines amid a climate of censorship, corporate takeovers, and economic instability. It’s no wonder, when media companies decide to partner with Amazon on art initiatives (cough, cough, Penske). Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia breaks down the survey results and what they can teach us about the future of independent, critical arts journalism.

Speaking of which, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports on a coalition of Tribal Nations opposing a bill that would threaten Native sites if Congress passes it. Longtime Angeleno Matt Stromberg considers an engrossing if occasionally overwrought book by James Cahill that explores the influential friendship between David Hockney and Betty Freeman, the arts patron at the center of one of his most recognizable paintings. And if that isn’t enough, Aaron Short shares a wry dispatch from the preview of the Art Dealers Association of America’s art fair in New York City — the tickets may have been $250 a pop, but at least there were unlimited dumplings and champagne to sweeten the deal?

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds

item.title: Sotheby’s $180 M. Van Gogh Sale Faces Eleventh-Hour Nazi-Era Restitution Claim - ARTnews.com
item.description:
With a $180 million painting by Vincent van Gogh due to go under the hammer Wednesday, Sotheby’s is pushing back against a last-minute restitution claim, citing details of a 1936 sale that the house says show the painting was sold voluntarily and for a good price.

The auction house told ARTnews that the archives of the art dealer Paul Cassirer confirm that van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), also known as Blossoming Chestnut Trees, sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, or about $22,000, in June 1936. Sotheby’s considers that a strong price for a van Gogh at the time. (Compare that to Verger avec cyprès (1888), a painting from the Paul Allen collection that fetched $117.2 million at Christie’s in 2022. That picture sold at Parke-Bernet in 1935 for $15,000.)

The new details come after the New York Times reported Friday that the heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher whose family fled Nazi Germany, had asked Sotheby’s to withdraw the painting from its November 18 auction. The heirs say the family was forced to sell the painting because of financial pressure brought on by Nazi persecution.

Their lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, challenged Sotheby’s to prove that the family received fair market value, according to an email shared with the New York Times, and would have sold the picture even if the Nazis had never come to power. “Otherwise,” he wrote, “no auction may take place.”

He also wrote that his client “is prepared to work toward a fair and just and just solution under the Washington Principles,” the guidelines accepted internationally for handling claims involving Nazi-looted art. ARTnews reached out to Schnabel for comment on evidence of duress, the family’s earlier restitution efforts, and what his client’s ideal outcome would be, but Schnabel did not answer before publication time.

The van Gogh is the star lot of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, assembled by the Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. The collection’s 12 Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings are expected to bring around $450 million. Sotheby’s has guaranteed the van Gogh, though the amount for that guarantee hasn’t been disclosed.

Sotheby’s wasn’t the only auction house eager to land the collection. According to people familiar with the negotiations, Christie’s also offered guarantees covering all the works, including the van Gogh. The figures are rumored to have been competitive with Sotheby’s and, in some cases, even higher.

For Sotheby’s, which has spent months promoting the collection, the timing could hardly be worse.

A Sale in Amsterdam

Samuel Fischer, who died in 1934, founded one of Germany’s most important publishing houses, with authors including Thomas Mann and Hermann Hesse. His son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, took over as the Nazis began banning many of the house’s authors. The family moved the business to Vienna in 1936, then fled Austria after the Nazi annexation in 1938. The Gestapo seized their Vienna home, library, and remaining art collection.

But the van Gogh’s history is different from that of the pictures the family lost in 1938.

According to the picture’s provenance, the family placed it with Cassirer’s Amsterdam gallery in 1932 or 1933, along with two Cézannes. It remained on consignment for nearly three years and traveled to both Rotterdam and Bern for exhibitions before being sold. The Netherlands was outside Nazi control at the time.

Luke Nikas, a lawyer representing Sotheby’s, told ARTnews that the van Gogh was sold to an independent buyer at fair market value. He also pointed out that the family held on to other paintings after the sale. Those were the works the Nazis eventually confiscated.

“The family had pursued and recovered works from the 1938 forced sale, but never the works they sold in 1936, such as this van Gogh,” Nikas said. He also described a postwar brochure published by Gottfried Bermann Fischer listing the paintings the family wanted to recover. Nikas said he has seen the document, and the van Gogh isn’t in it.

The two Cézannes tell another interesting part of the story. One is now at the Harvard Art Museums, where it has been on public display for years without a claim from the Fischer heirs. The other was offered at Christie’s in 2007, and again in 2017 when it sold for almost $6 million. In 2007, Gisela Bermann Fischer, who handled the family’s art claims until her death in 2014, told Christie’s that she wouldn’t oppose the sale.

There was a catch, though. In the same letter, as reported by the Times, she specifically reserved the right to challenge the sales of other family paintings she believed had been sold under duress. Sotheby’s told ARTnews that it had looked into the 2007 Cézanne sale but didn’t know about that reservation, which appeared in confidential correspondence between Bermann Fischer and Christie’s.

Sotheby’s restitution team has come in for scrutiny, too. As Julie Brener Davich noted in her Substack, the Appraisal, and as the New York Times reported in a follow-up Sunday, Lucian Simmons, who established Sotheby’s restitution department in 1997 and ran it for years, left for the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2024. Richard Aronowitz, who headed Sotheby’s European restitution work for 15 years, joined Christie’s in 2022. Both were also specialists in Impressionist and modern art. Two people familiar with Sotheby’s restitution operation told ARTnews that the department has almost doubled since it was run by Simmons.

What Counts as Duress?

The question here is whether a painting sold outside Nazi Germany to an independent buyer and at a good price can still be considered a forced sale. Nikas says New York law distinguishes between the terrible conditions Jews faced under the Nazis and a sale in which the buyer actually pressured the seller.

He pointed to two cases involving Picassos sold by Jewish families during the Nazi era.

In Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art, a federal judge ruled in 2018 that a 1938 sale didn’t meet the legal standard for duress. An appeals court upheld the dismissal in 2019, though for a different reason: the family had waited too long to bring its claim. In Bennigson v. Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, a New York judge similarly ruled in 2024 that economic pressure caused by Nazi persecution wasn’t enough to establish duress when the buyer hadn’t contributed to it. The dismissal was upheld on appeal in 2025, again because of the delay.

That last point is interesting because Congress changed the rules earlier this year. In April, lawmakers amended the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act, or HEAR Act, eliminating laches, a legal defense that had allowed courts to throw out restitution claims because heirs had waited too long to pursue them. That makes it harder for museums, collectors, and auction houses to win qualifying cases simply by arguing that too much time has passed. It doesn’t change what counts as a forced sale, however.

Nikas said that distinction is crucial. Congress removed a defense based on delay, he said, but left the legal test for duress alone. He believes the 1936 sale fails that test.

Judd Grossman, a New York art lawyer who isn’t involved in the dispute but has experience with restitution cases, thinks the change has tipped the balance considerably toward claimants. “With this year’s amendments to the HEAR Act eliminating the equitable laches defense, which had prevented heirs from unfairly sitting on their rights before making a claim, the pendulum has swung dramatically in favor of claimants regardless of whether they have ever taken steps to vindicate their rights,” Grossman told ARTnews.

“Whatever the merits of the underlying title dispute, under this new statutory regime, we will see more of this sort of gamesmanship by claimants waiting to the very last minute to come forward before seeking their slice of the pie.”

With a $180 million van Gogh heading to auction Wednesday, Sotheby’s finds itself having to negotiate with the heirs of its former owner, or risk upsetting the biggest sale of the season.

Schnabel isn’t new to restitution claims. In 2016, he and provenance researcher Monika Tatzkow were already investigating Nazi-era losses involving paintings by Piet Mondrian when they approached the artist’s heirs and offered to look into other works. The family hired them, and their research eventually led to a restitution claim against the Philadelphia Museum of Art, according to a 2022 federal court opinion recounting the heirs’ allegations. Whether Schnabel approached the Fischers this time, or they approached him, isn’t clear.

Which brings us to the timing. Sotheby’s says it first heard from representatives of the Fischer heirs on Thursday morning, November 12. The Times contacted the auction house the following morning and published its story that evening. By then, the van Gogh had been publicly advertised for more than six weeks. The auction was only five days away.

Nikas questioned why the claim had arrived so close to the sale–the sale was first publicized in early October–though he said Sotheby’s was taking it seriously. The heirs may have good grounds for questioning what happened in 1936, but the timing gave Sotheby’s little room to respond before the allegations became public, which could have been the point.

There’s another question, too. Schnabel has asked Sotheby’s to establish not only that the family received a good price, but that it would have sold the painting even if the Nazis had never come to power. This may be difficult to prove in the case of a transaction that took place 90 years ago.

For now, Sotheby’s says the painting is still scheduled to be offered Wednesday night. The Blaquier family, meanwhile, says it is willing to talk. In a statement to ARTnews, the family said it had owned the painting for decades and respected the historical concerns involved.

“While the information available to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, the family welcomes constructive dialogue with the Fischer heirs and supports efforts to reach a mutually satisfactory resolution,” the family said.

Whether that happens before Wednesday remains to be seen.

item.title: Europol Warns of More Aggressive Museum Heists as Thieves Change Tactics and Targets - ARTnews.com
item.description:
It seems like news of new museum robberies just keeps coming, particularly in the months following the brazen Louvre heist one year ago. In an attempt to shed light on the phenomenon, Europol published a study in August, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists, which examines key trends within these more recent crimes, as reported earlier by The Art Newspaper.

What does Europol tell us? For one, the old notion that museum thefts are generally non-violent, or use stealthy tactics such as replacing precious jewels or artworks with convincing fakes, is no longer the case. “Offenders are adopting more direct and confrontational approaches,” as well as “a growing use of force” to break into museums and display cases using tools like sledgehammers, axes, crowbars, and sometimes explosives, states the report. On some occasions, museum workers have been intimidated with weapons, but also directly assaulted. According to the report, Louvre staff and visitors were threatened by the men who broke into the museum during its opening hours on October 19, 2025, and successfully fled with over $102 million worth of the country’s crown jewels.

The kinds of things getting stolen are also changing. In the last few years, thieves have increasingly been going for precious stones and metals such as gold, which can be melted down, cut, or taken apart from their casings and sold without a trace. Plus, these materials attract attention due to a “perception that museum security measures are less robust than those in jewelry stores.”

Chinese cultural artifacts have also become hot targets. These include examples such as 12th- and 13th-century porcelain jars and vases from the Ming Dynasty, plus colored enamels on bronze vases from both the Ming and Qing Dynasties. The report affirms these Chinese cultural goods are in high demand and “are likely to be easily sold on the art market.”

As for the perpetrators, they tend to have a history of involvement with other types of crime, and increasingly, coordinate with accomplices on an “ad hoc basis,” or without prior connection. In other words, these are not necessarily organized networks built around a core group or leader. As a result, investigators have theorized that criminals may be randomly recruiting “low-level” accomplices or perpetrators to break into museums.

As for the frequency of museum heists, the report does not mention whether they have gone up. Jean-Yves Goriou, head of the EU Organized Crime Unit in Europol’s European Serious and Organized Crime Centre (ESOCC), did confirm in an interview with TAN that, “We have observed a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023.”

However, that view was contrasted with that of another expert, Robert Read, the head of art and private clients at Hiscox Insurance. “In the sense of volume of crimes [against museums], there’s not been a change,” he said. Meanwhile, Julian Radcliffe, the director of the Art Loss Register, observes that “A lot of these trends [in the Europol report] are not new, but they’re arguably occurring on a more pronounced or regular scale.” It sure feels that way.

item.title: Sotheby’s Hedreen Auction Proceeds Will Repay Loan, Not Fund University Museum: Report - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A $300 million art donation to Seattle University has been revealed to be more complex than originally reported.

On Monday, Sotheby’s will begin selling approximately 50 works from the collection amassed by Seattle real estate developer and philanthropist Richard “Dick” Hedreen, previously billed as the “largest art gift ever” to a US university. Hedreen said in September that the sale did not mean the promised gift was falling through. Rather, he suggested, the proceeds would help furnish Seattle University’s new art museum, where the collection was eventually expected to hang.

Records newly reported on by The Seattle Times, however, tell a different story: The works are being sold not to fund the museum, but to pay off a debt secured against the collection — a debt Hedreen says stands between him and fulfilling his pledge to the university.

What was originally framed as a donation, in reality, was a pledge: Hedreen, whose firm R.C. Hedreen Co. owns the Grand Hyatt among other Seattle properties, retained the right to buy and sell works from the collection until the gift was finalized. The Sotheby’s auction is expected to generate at least $100 million across a series of sales. As of writing, the overall value of the artwork set for Seattle University is unclear.

The sale spans an expansive sweep of art history. Works by Willem de Kooning, Rashid Johnson, Amy Sherald, and Jonas Wood will be offered alongside Old Masters by Bronzino, Jacopo Pontormo, Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, and Thomas Gainsborough. Leading Sotheby’s offerings is Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990), estimated at $20 million to $30 million. Cecily Brown’s 12-foot-wide Untitled (Shipwreck) (2017), estimated at $7 million to $10 million, is another highlight.

A news release from Seattle University stated: “Hedreen has given the university the renowned Hedreen Collection (named for himself and his late wife Elizabeth ‘Betty’ Ann Petri Hedreen, a Seattle University alumna) valued at $300 million, along with $25 million in seed funding to develop the museum.”

However, the Seattle Times reported that records show that the “seed funding” was actually provided through the private sale of a de Kooning painting. Estimated in 2024 to be worth $25 million, the work fetched $17 million.

The Sotheby’s sale proceeds will instead go toward paying off an outstanding loan secured against the collection. The borrowing dates to 2012, when Hedreen first pledged several artworks, including a pieces by Francis Bacon, de Kooning and David Hockney, as collateral for a Goldman Sachs loan. In 2025, that financing was replaced with a Bank of America loan secured by approximately 44 major artworks.

R.C. Hedreen Co. President David Thyer confirmed that the Sotheby’s sale is tied to financial pressures in the hotel and real estate markets. Income generated by the company’s properties, he said, is insufficient to repay the loan “in any reasonably foreseeable time frame.”

ARTnews has contacted Sotheby’s for comment.

Richard Hedreen’s son, Guy, said in a statement that his family’s “commitment to Seattle University has not changed.” His father, Guy added, “is not selling works from his collection in order to spend money on himself” or his business. Rather, the auction reflects his commitment to the university “by removing a debt that prevents him from translating his pledge intentions into an outright gift.”

Construction on the new art museum, originally scheduled to begin this past summer, has been pushed to 2027 as the project awaits permits. Designed by local architect Tom Kundig, the museum is intended to permanently house the Hedreen collection, alongside rotating exhibitions and academic programming.

Scott K. McClellan, Seattle University’s vice president for university affairs, said the school continues to believe the collection “presents a significant opportunity for the university, community and our broader vision for the arts.” He reiterated the “shared intention of Mr. Hedreen and the university” that Seattle University ultimately receive a collection of museum-quality works commensurate with the collection that formed the basis of the original commitment.

McClellan added that it had been “reasonable” for the university to expect Hedreen’s loan to be paid off by 2028, when the museum was originally scheduled for completion.

item.title: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week.

The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.

“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.

item.title: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “Beverly Hills Housewife,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.

Critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his new book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.

item.title: Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Tribal organizations are urging legislators to halt the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would speed up the permitting and review processes of major infrastructure projects and could severely undermine tribal sovereignty over sacred and culturally significant sites.

The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966.

The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process. The bill text also curtails several other environmental acts, such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, and pushes for shorter review timelines, the loosening of protections of sacred lands, and less federal oversight.

item.title: Long-Lost Charles Le Brun Painting Returns to the New Palace in Potsdam - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Lost for more than 75 years, a painting by French Baroque artist Charles Le Brun (1619–1690) is now returning to the New Palace in Potsdam’s Sanssouci Park. The news was first reported by the German Press Agency (dpa) following a statement by the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation Berlin-Brandenburg (SPSG).

Court painter to Louis XIV after 1661 and the designer most responsible for the opulent style of the Sun King’s monarchy, Le Brun created the work, a depiction of a sleeping Christ Child with the Holy Family, around 1655. It was acquired in the 1700s by King Frederick the Great (Frederick II) of Prussia for the New Palace, where it hung in one of the guest apartments.

In 1942, to protect it from Allied bombings, much of the art at the Picture Gallery of Sanssouci and the New Palace, including Le Brun’s painting, was evacuated some 60 miles northwest to Schloss Rheinsberg.

On April 29, 1945, the Red Army entered Rheinsberg. Russian troops occupied the building, and a short time later the majority of the paintings housed in the Schloss Rheinsberg were sent to the Soviet Union. However, according to the SPSG, not all of the works arrived there, with some entering private collections in Rheinsberg under “convoluted circumstances.”

Le Brun’s painting was documented as being at Schloss Rheinsberg until July 30, 1945. After that, according to a spokesperson from the foundation, the painting vanished—until it resurfaced at a Berlin auction house in 2021.

The return was made possible by the support of the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation and the Friends of the Prussian Palaces Association. On November 18, 2026 at 2:30 p.m., the “Holy Family” will be unveiled in the Upper Red Chambers of the New Palace.

item.title: The Alchemical Possibilities of an Artist-Poet Collaboration - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In 1982, Puerto Rican artist Papo Colo installed a book-shaped sculpture in the courtyard of El Museo del Barrio in Harlem. Commissioned as part of David Hammons’s Art in the Park program, it unfurled like an accordion across a series of 8-by-4-foot plywood panels co-authored by nearly 40 invited New York artists and poets. Four decades later, seven of those panels form the basis of Octopus and Others, an exhibition that addresses the porous boundary between the word and the image within the more experimental scenes of production from the ‘80s through today.

The first panel in the exhibition is by Colo himself and gestures toward the alchemical, even transcendent possibilities unleashed through the collaboration of artists and poets across distances, languages, and generations. “English Spanish $ Spanglish,” Colo scribbles in white paint against the black-coated plywood. “Vivas poetas individuales X-formed by Colo’s ceremony into collective.”

item.title: Fake UK Artist Visas Are Being Offered for $132,000, New Investigation Finds - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Several companies have been helping migrants apply for UK visas under the government’s Global Talent program by creating fake art portfolios, complete with fake published art criticism and art news, according to a new investigation published by the BBC Friday.

Nigerian art critic Molara Wood told the publication that she had found her name attached to fake online reviews praising the works of two obscure artists, just one instance of the materials created.

“There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists,” Wood told the BBC. Following the BBC’s investigation, two Nigerian men’s visas are in the process of being revoked, according to the Home Office. The two claimed to be fine art photographers in their visa applications.

One BBC reporter went undercover to research the companies offering packages through the Global Talent program. The firm said it could supply the reporter with artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation. The reporter had been reassured that the “fully inclusive” would grant them a visa without refusal—the package was priced at more than £100,000 ($132,000). The Home Office told the BBC that the company the reporter had dug out was already under investigation. A spokesperson for the Home Office said that they “will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system” and the “home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused.”

The government’s Global Talent program was launched in 2020 and was designed to attract creative workers, including scientists and artists. However, in recent years, it has become a way for companies to target wealthy migrants looking to move without going through the official route, which has become challenging in the UK following new immigration laws.

In another case, a woman said she worked with a company to help her secure a talent visa through the tech route. The company had used fabricated evidence for her application, including a fictitious mentoring award and materials falsely suggesting that she had been a keynote speaker at an event. In the end, her application was rejected.

The companies offering talent visas have been targeting all nationalities. The BBC found two companies in its investigation: iCareer Consultancy and its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, based out of London’s corporate hub, Canary Wharf, offering fake artwork and immigration advice. During a call with an undercover BBC reporter, an iCareer consultant said that four of his clients obtained a visa this year and that they can supply the reporter with an employee to pose as a client and network for them at gallery openings. The company also said that for £28,000 ($37,000), they can offer a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, boosting their chances of securing a visa.

iCareer told the BBC through its lawyers that it strongly denied “offering any visa services whatsoever” and that meeting with the consultant “was not authorized by iCareer.”

“We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him,” the company said.

item.title: ‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District - Colossal
item.description:
In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated places.” When it comes to preserving important historical locations, such as monuments, parks, and buildings, a new interactive public art installation asks, “what happens when preservation itself is endangered?”

The Sacred Ordinary is an initiative organized by 1504, a production studio based in Birmingham that emphasizes in-depth storytelling to connect people with meaningful, human-focused services and experiences. The participatory artwork is presented in collaboration with the National Parks Conservation Association, which aims to protect U.S. national parks for future generations.

In early 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that mandated the removal of some National Park Service signage relating to slavery, the LGBTQ+ community, climate change, and more, a move that erases histories inextricable from the nation’s identity. (The current administration has also blocked millions in funding for numerous parks and disrupted services.)

In Birmingham, the Civil Rights District is formally designated a national monument, comprising neighborhoods that Black people historically called home and where Jim Crow laws authorized segregation until the 1960s. The Civil Rights Movement reached a nexus here when activists Fred Shuttlesworth, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Ralph Abernathy, among many others, organized nonviolent marches in 1963, known today as the Birmingham Campaign. Police turned their dogs on demonstrators and used fire hoses on children. A bombing at a Baptist church killed four young Black girls.

The Sacred Ordinary venerates access to things most of us take for granted: the ability to shop at any store, attend the nearest school, walk around any neighborhood, and sit at the front of the bus. The exhibition is installed around-the-clock, but by day, elements of the installation comprise vintage yet mundane objects that one typically walks by without giving a second thought.

A huge midcentury television rests on an open lawn, and a red newspaper vending box for The Birmingham News, which ceased its print publication in 2012, advertises 25 cents per copy. Additional sites include a characteristically blue U.S. Postal Service mailbox and a walk-in telephone booth. Sheets of paper with tear-off tabs posted around town invite participants to learn more by texting a phone number. If you text “HERE” to the number, you’ll be directed to a starting point and an otherwise nondescript yellow fire hydrant.

In scavenger-hunt style, visitors are prompted to enter the year stamped on the unit, and if it’s between 5 and 8 p.m., the sequence of texted prompts doubles as a multimedia self-guided tour of Birmingham’s Civil Rights District like you’ve never seen it: the television screen, mailbox, phone booth, and more begin to glow once the sun has set.

“Birmingham, Alabama, is known around the world for such places—sites of civil rights history that many regard as sacred and that connect us to something larger than ourselves. But today, that memory is endangered,” 1504 says in a statement. “Aging infrastructure, the passing of a generation of foot soldiers, and federal efforts to erase chapters of American history raise an urgent question: if institutions alone cannot sustain history, what role can the public play in caring for sacred sites?”

Rather than center primarily on signage, The Sacred Ordinary focuses on objects associated with civic life in the mid-20th century, evoking collective memories and providing touchpoints for younger generations for whom boxy televisions, printed newspapers, and telephone booths feel distant from today’s experiences. Emblematic of the way news and information spread before the internet and smartphones, the objects confront visitors with not only the realities of how people organized and communicated during that time but also how those memories are preserved today. Even without didactics, objects and places carry meaning that no one can simply delete.

The tour opens with a narration by actor André Holland, who played a fundamental role in preserving a historic theater in nearby Bessemer, Alabama, and 1504 has dedicated the installation to Birmingham-based artist Joe Minter. The Sacred Ordinary continues nightly through December 13, with accompanying guided walks and other programs scheduled in the meantime. Learn more on the project’s website, and explore the studio’s work on Instagram. You might also be interested in “The Praise House,” directed by 1504’s Tyler Jones.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article ‘The Sacred Ordinary’ Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham’s Civil Rights District appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: Seán Doran’s ‘Crimson Star’ Tours the Raging Surface of the Sun - Colossal
item.description:
Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. The footage-like video tours the sun and reveals its fiery surface complete with brilliant solar flares, all depicted in a distinctive crimson.

To create the film, Doran attributed various pinks and reds to different wavelengths, creating an alluring interpretation of the fiery orb. Doran stitched together NASA’s captures, or more accurately, he says, the images were “conformed, repaired, graded, blended, rescaled and retimed” into a seamless film. “Crimson Star” is one of several astral projects he’s undertaken in recent years, and you can keep up with his latest works on YouTube. (via Kottke)

item.title: A Toolkit for a Liberated Art World - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“Radical politics,” “marginalized communities,” “feminist art” … If you see these terms peppering wall labels at a major museum, there’s an excellent chance the institution behaves in direct opposition to those values and groups. Scholars Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon, who were also among the organizers of the historic Strike MoMA protests in 2021, know this pattern all too well. It’s part of the neoliberal capture of art institutions, which Italian curator and activist Marco Baravalle lays bare in his new book, The Battleground of Art. Read on for a review by Husain and Dhillon, who write that it’s a toolkit for building a better, freer art world.

Meanwhile, in the United States, that art world finds itself at a crucial turning point. In the wake of the midterm elections, longtime nonprofit arts leader Jasmine Wahi reminds us that the fight is only beginning. She opines today about the importance of holding Democratic officials accountable not just for redressing the damage inflicted by the Trump administration, but also for taking its responsibility to artists and culture workers seriously. “Rebuilding the same inadequate baseline is not enough,” she explains.

More in the news today, including public backlash against Egypt’s arrest of the editor of an independent publication and San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato’s resistance against Silicon Valley and enshittifcation through his quietly subversive art. Heaven knows we could all use more of that.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins

In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition. | Jasmine Wahi

item.title: How Does an Artist Know When She’s Done? A Major Marisa Merz Retrospective Turns the Question on Its Head - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Italian artist Marisa Merz (1926–2019) was famously camera-shy. In rare snapshots, such as a captivating photograph taken by Claudio Abate at her 1975 solo show in Rome, she would retreat from the camera’s gaze. Before Abate’s camera, Merz appears clad in her woven nylon Scarpette (Little Shoes), 1968, her back to him as she gazes out an open window at the moon.

The turn away is emblematic of Merz’s artistic ethos writ large. As she once wrote, in a 1975 issue of Data Arte magazine, “The artist is already an established role, like the wife, the son. But I don’t go along with these roles.”

Merz was the only woman affiliated with Arte Povera, a loose movement christened in 1967 by curator Germano Celant that rejected the commodification of art and celebrated presence and materiality through nontraditional media and process-based practices. Even within this iconoclast milieu, she remained an outlier, not only for her inscription of domestic labor into her work—in her 1967 film The Count, she is seen in her kitchen sorting beans—but also for her use of figuration from the 1970s onward. Her unruly aluminum installations, paraffin pools, and woven forms were overlooked in the 1960s and 1970s, but she has gained wider recognition in recent years. Since the 1990s, major exhibitions of her work have been staged across Europe and the US, and in 2013, the Venice Biennale honored her with a Golden Lion.

Still, Merz remains evasive even as she enters the spotlight. A sprawling and polyphonic retrospective titled “Marisa Merz: La danza delle ore (The Dance of the Hours)” has taken over three Turin institutions on the centenary of her birth. Yet despite its exhaustive review of more than five decades of her work, she remains enigmatic. The Galleria d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea Torino (GAM) emphasizes her superposition of studio and home; the Fondazione Merz focuses on her material experiments; and the Castello di Rivoli explores her metaphysical engagement with space. All the while, Merz’s elusive central themes—transparency, metamorphosis, and alchemy—recur throughout.

True to the retrospective’s title, the suite of exhibitions doesn’t follow a chronological itinerary, if only because to do so is nearly impossible. Her biography remains shrouded in mystery. These are the known facts of her life before 1960: Born in Turin to a father employed by Fiat, she studied dance and later modeled in other artists’ studios. Even after garnering critical attention, she rarely titled or dated her compositions and struggled to lay them to rest. The title of her first and best-known installation, The Living Sculpture (1966), says it all, encoding her belief that completion is concomitant to a kind of death.

This unsettled attitude manifests in a provisional quality that prevails across the works on view. The Living Sculpture is a tentacular, sewn-aluminum work that originally dangled claustrophobically from the ceilings of her home and now hangs in glittering fragments at GAM and Castello di Rivoli. Her series of knobby clay “Testine (Little Heads),” made from the 1970s to the 2010s, are unfired and sometimes retain the rough corners with which they were cut in bricklike masses from a larger block of clay. Her abstracted faces, painted and drawn on paper, wood, and alabaster, are warped and blurred as if in motion; one untitled and undated graphite physiognomy rearranges itself in whirling lines of vortex-like eyes.

Merz, like her Arte Povera peers, was frustrated by fixity and drawn to materials that morph across time. Perhaps appropriately, the curators have displayed works that may be unfinished and come straight from the studio; whether she planned to continue them will never be known. Notes on hotel stationery and Post-its remain tacked, taped, and clipped directly onto her drawings and paintings, variably describing the emotions she hoped to capture (for example, “expressive and polished”), quoting from literature (one composition glosses Hölderlin’s final poem), or simply logging dimensions. There is a sense that Merz might yet return with needle, pencil, or brush and pick up where she left off.

As if to show how an idea remains unfixed, persisting and evolving as later generations take it on, the exhibitions stage encounters between Merz and contemporary women artists—including Leonor Antunes, Thea Djordjadze, and Miriam Cahn—whose work shares affinities with hers. Tacita Dean was commissioned to produce a body of film and photographs in Merz’s home and studio. The results include a 16 mm film diptych Via Milano 13 (2026) capturing scenes from Merz’s apartment near Turin’s Porta Palazzo market. In slow frames, we see a honeycombed assemblage of cardboard cylinders from rolls of toilet paper and paper towels; a chorus of “Testine” arranged on the spiraling table in her husband’s old studio; a painted, blue-haired visage with livid red lips fastened on a wall, its double mirrored upside-down in a glass surface below. Hung in constellated installations at GAM and Fondazione Merz, a complementary series of photographs likewise opens Merz’s private world to our curious eyes, often capturing works in situ among furniture and family photographs before their displacement to the exhibitions’ airy galleries. The film and images verge on invasion, contravening Merz’s injunction against photographic capture—except, of course, for the fact of the artist’s absence, palpable in Dean’s meditative, static shots.

Leaving this suite of exhibitions, I find Merz’s practice is even more fugitive than before. I am not the first critic to encounter this difficulty. Writing on her work for Artforum in 1992, Celant reflected, “The instant it is defined, it flees.” Like the artist herself, Merz’s works are chimerical, morphing with the shifting light, blurring at the edges of the frame, slipping out of sight.

item.title: Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic, urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue.

“MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Batista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon.

“Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Batista continues.

The letter makes reference to three sexual assault and misconduct accusations brought forth against the billionaire, all of which Black denies. One of the lawsuits was discontinued by the plaintiff, and an earlier lawsuit was dismissed by the court. A third lawsuit was allowed to move forward after a judge imposed a sanction. UltraViolet said it has not received a response from Spielberg's representatives.

Black left his role as CEO of his private equity firm Apollo Global Management in 2021, when news broke that he paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein’s first conviction for soliciting sex from a minor. Even though he stepped down as MoMA board chairman that same year, after Hyperallergic published an open letter signed by over 150 artists calling for his removal, Black remains a MoMA board trustee.

Public scrutiny of Black intensified in September, after the US House of Representatives unanimously approved a resolution to hold the MoMA trustee in contempt of Congress for defying subpoenas in an Epstein investigation. This month, Black sued California Representative Robert Garcia for defamation over public comments such as "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”

Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner, who initially posted an open letter to Spielberg on her Instagram, said she was “amazed” by the public response.

“Steven Spielberg has made his career making stories about the dignity of women and children,” Gardner told Hyperallergic at tonight's protest. “It's totally disgusting that he's accepting an award [at the film center named after Leon Black], who's currently in contempt of Congress for not producing NDAs and his involvement in the Epstein files.”

Last month, Gardner co-performed a staged reading of former Barclays CEO and JP Morgan executive Jes Staley's deposition on Epstein to the United States House Oversight Committee in July.

At this evening's protest, others carried signs pointing to Black's connections to pro-Israel and Zionist organizations. Black has reportedly donated money to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which denies that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and Birthright Israel, which is accused of serving as a propaganda campaign for the Israeli government.

“I can personally say I'm Jewish and it's specifically because of my Jewish values that we're here. Never again means never again for anyone,” one demonstrator, Janet Goodman-Clarke, told Hyperallergic. “Leon Black not only is a Zionist, but he's also named ad nauseam in the Epstein files.”

MoMA has not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment.

Artists, activists, and Epstein survivors have repeatedly gathered in front of MoMA demanding his ousting. Among those in attendance at today's action was Katie Fuller, arts educator and founder of the Time and Memory Project, who staged a separate protest calling for Black's removal in front of the museum with her sister in September.

Last month, Fuller teamed up with Epstein survivors, UltraViolet, and the Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts, to illustrate the extent of Epstein's network. The free, mobile installation displayed a timeline of President Donald Trump’s relationship with Epstein and contains thousands of books' worth of the released so-called “Epstein Files,” in which Black was mentioned over 8,500 times.

That protest included Dani Bensky, a dancer, educator, and Epstein survivor from 2004 to 2005. A few weeks after the action, Bensky wrote an op-ed for Hyperallergic condemning Black’s board position as “one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.”

Besides his investments in MoMA, Black has held enormous sway in the art world. In a newly released book by William D. Cohan, Black disclosed plans to convert the Woolworth Mansion into a tax-beneficial art foundation, which is expected to house works from his estimated $5 billion art collection, an asset that Epstein helped leverage as bank collateral.

Gardner said she had one simple message for the attendees of tonight’s benefit gala: “If you know, you're human garbage. And if you didn't know, you can't say that after tonight, because we're out here saying hi to everybody with our signs.”

item.title: Artnet’s Kalshi Partnership Faces Swift Backlash Online, But Advisers Are More Mixed - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The art world, as much as we love it, has never been accused of lacking opportunities for speculation. But apparently “there’s room for one more, honey.“

On Wednesday, Artnet announced that it had partnered with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that lets users bet on everything from election results to sporting events. Artnet will become Kalshi’s official art partner, helping select markets and supplying the auction data used to determine which bets pay out.

The reaction on Instagram was swift and, let’s say, not particularly kind.

“How convenient. Now you can misunderstand art from anywhere,” wrote one commenter.

“Listen y’all there simply weren’t enough ways to artificially inflate an artist’s market and destroy their career before they turn 30,” wrote another.

Then came perhaps the most inspired comment, which may be a prediction of Artnet’s next move on the chessboard: “UFC x ARTNET! ARTNET JOE ROGAN.”

The partnership comes seven months after Artnet, the auction-data and media company, announced a mergerwith the online art brokerage Artsy. The combined company is led by chairman Andrew Wolff, CEO of Beowolff Capital, which acquired majority stakes in both companies over the past year.

It also comes just days before New York’s marquee November sales, which will offer plenty of chances to put the partnership to the test. Kalshi introduced art-related prediction markets in May and already offers contracts on individual paintings, entire collections, and whether artists will break their auction records.

Take Yoshitomo Nara’s Candy Blue Night (2001), which is headed to Sotheby’s on November 16. Users can trade contracts on whether the painting will sell for more than $6 million or $7 million. They can also trade on major works by Francis Bacon, Andy Warhol, and Roy Lichtenstein that are coming up for sale.

For now, the money changing hands in Kalshi’s art markets is dwarfed by the value of the objects being bet on. On Thursday, a market for Sotheby’s Blaquier-Arrieta Collection showed a roughly 52 percent probability that the sale would exceed $500 million. At the time, it had attracted just $372 in trading volume.

Still, the idea of making money from an auction without having to buy anything has its attractions.

Wendy Cromwell, founder of the advisory firm Cromwell Art and a former Sotheby’s contemporary-art specialist, saw some promise in the idea but also reasons for concern.

“I do think it’s a way for people to participate in the community,” she said. She added that she meant people who are engaged with the art world, follow artists, and understand their markets, even if they aren’t collectors themselves.

But Cromwell also saw a potential problem: the advantage held by people with access to information the public doesn’t have.

“It’s going to be extraordinarily tempting for everybody because everyone in the art world has inside knowledge,” she said.

Philip Hoffman, founder and chairman of the Fine Art Group, was less enthusiastic. “I can’t see that it’s a great use to collectors,” he said. In his view, there’s no reliable way to predict the prices of major works, where personal preference, provenance, condition, and the whims of the wealthy can render even the most carefully considered valuations irrelevant.

Results for more ordinary works, he said, can be relatively predictable. The top of the market is another matter. “People get carried away if they truly want it, and there’s no price,” he said.

Hoffman recalled once guaranteeing a Willem de Kooning painting that everyone expected to fetch substantially more than $10 million. Then the stock market fell, bidders disappeared, and he was left owning the painting himself. He eventually sold it for $9.7 million, taking a $300,000 loss. In other words, even knowing who intends to bid is no guarantee of knowing what will happen when the auctioneer raises the gavel.

There are also more troubling possibilities.

The art market runs on information that isn’t always available to the public. Auction-house specialists usually know how many bidders are registered for a sale. Dealers and advisors may know who is interested in a painting, how badly they want it, and what they’re prepared to pay. Guarantors may already have a financial stake in a work before it reaches the auction block.

That’s an obvious problem for a prediction market. A casual participant might have access to auction estimates, past sales results, and whatever enthusiasm is circulating on social media. Someone closer to the sale, meanwhile, might know about confidential expressions of interest, guarantees, or the number of absentee bidders. The two would hardly be working with the same information.

Then again, access to sensitive information isn’t limited to senior specialists. Junior employees who help keep the wheels of commerce turning could also be privy to confidential bidding information, giving them an advantage over ordinary traders.

When Kalshi first moved into the art market in May, Christie’s and Phillips told ARTnews that they have robust policies governing the use of confidential information and participation in activities that present a conflict of interest. Both said those policies cover prediction markets. Sotheby’s declined to comment at the time.

For its part, Kalshi prohibits trading on material nonpublic information. Its rules for artwork-price contracts also bar certain insiders from participating, including consignors, bidders, guarantors, and auction-house employees involved in a sale. But identifying those people and enforcing those restrictions in a business built on discretion is a challenge of its own.

The question I can’t stop turning over: Could prediction markets influence the auctions themselves? One can imagine a feedback loop in which speculative enthusiasm on prediction markets drives expectations higher and sways real buyers. A collector who sees overwhelming confidence that a picture will blow past its estimate might begin to second-guess an advisor’s valuation. Dealers or other interested parties might also see an opening to stoke enthusiasm for an artist’s market.

There’s another intriguing possibility. Might collectors use prediction contracts to offset some of their auction spending, effectively hedging their exposure to a purchase? Or might they look for gaps between the expectations reflected on Kalshi and what they believe artworks will actually bring at auction?

But there’s a catch. Kalshi’s rules prohibit people who can influence an auction’s outcome from betting on it. And with so little money being wagered so far, there isn’t much to be made anyway.

For now, the gap between multimillion-dollar auctions and prediction markets with little real money on the line suggests that Kalshi’s art offerings are more experiment than alternative financial market.

Still, Artnet’s involvement adds another dimension. The company will help identify subjects for prediction markets and provide data from its Price Database to verify the outcomes. Kalshi will continue to design the contracts and operate the exchange. Artnet has said its newsroom will not be involved in creating the markets or verifying results.

For Cromwell, the important question is whether anyone should treat these predictions as a serious measure of what art is worth.

“I think it’s a fool’s game to listen to prediction markets,” she said. “If you’re spending lots and lots of money, you should do your own research and have your own convictions about what you want to spend.”

item.title: How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture - Hyperallergic
item.description:
We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.

Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.

Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

item.title: How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint - Colossal
item.description:
Looking at the serene paintings that emerge from Sky Glabush’ s studio, it’s easy to feel a soft breeze sliding off bare summer shoulders or hear the crunch of leaves underfoot, their parched fibers reverberating across the autumn landscape. Transportive and atmospherically charged, the landscapes harness the allure of texture to draw the viewer in and invite them to stay a while.

Raised on the west coast of British Columbia and currently based in rural Ontario, Glabush has long been attuned to the natural world. He often identifies the feelings he associates with a particular place and translates that through color and intuitive interpretations of the terrain: the spindly, strangely straight tree trunks of a forest, for example, or the ways a sunflower echoes the radial form of the sun.

Glabush typically utilizes limited palettes that adhere to just one or two color families. He also mixes oil paint with granular particles, sand being the most common, although he’s used crushed quartz and raw pigment. Originally, the idea of combining materials emerged because the artist wanted, he says, to “obliterate the image… But I realized it didn’t destroy the image. It was still present and humming under that surface layer. So it gave me the freedom of deciding what I wanted to hold on to or what I wanted to erase.”

Adding and removing has since become integral to Glabush’s practice, which involves adding thin stains of paint and turpentine to the point of the painting becoming relief-like. He tends to begin with an architectural structure that anchors the work. Sometimes a grid and others a radial arrangement, the foundational patterns inform each resulting layer. Color, though, is always “the unifying principle, it is the energy and dynamism, it is the element of surprise. Each painting often goes through several iterations of colour before deciding on a direction.” 

Although he’s worked with other materials in the past and has particularly enjoyed carving, the conventions and limitations of painting always drew him back. “That period of experimentation with sculpture allowed me to treat my paintings in a more physically robust and experimental way. But even during my most experimental period, I saw myself as a painter and wanted to find a way to express myself within that language,” he tells Colossal.

Some of the works here will be on view in Glabush’s solo exhibition, If the Wild Bird Could Speak, on view from November 20 to January 9 at Alison Jacques in London. Until then, explore more of his paintings on Instagram.
